sections.title: Newborn deaths in Sudan and the national plan (SuNAP)

read.text: Neonatal health remains a critical global public health priority, as the period around birth carries the highest risk of mortality for both mothers and newborns. Globally, nearly 1.3 million fresh stillbirths and approximately 1 million neonatal deaths occur each year in close temporal association with childbirth. The majority of these deaths are preventable through timely, high-quality, and evidence-based interventions delivered during pregnancy, labour, childbirth, and the early postnatal period, with particular attention to small and sick newborns.

In Sudan, the burden of neonatal mortality and stillbirths remains unacceptably high and represents a major contributor to under-five mortality. In 2023, Sudan’s neonatal mortality rate (NMR) was estimated at 24.8 per 1,000 live births, translating into approximately 41,690 neonatal deaths annually. In parallel, the stillbirth rate was estimated at 21.51 per 1,000 total births, corresponding to nearly 36,973 stillbirths each year. These figures reflect not only the magnitude of the problem but also the persistent gaps in access to quality maternal and newborn health services, particularly in fragile, conflict-affected, and humanitarian settings.

Recognizing this burden, the Federal Ministry of Health has prioritized newborn survival as a national agenda through the development and implementation of the Sudan Newborn Action Plan (SuNAP) 2022–2030, aligned with global commitments under the Sustainable Development Goals. SuNAP sets ambitious but achievable targets, aiming for 50% of Sudanese states to achieve 12 or fewer neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births, and 60% of states to reach 12 or fewer stillbirths per 1,000 total births by 2030, with a strong emphasis on equity, including populations affected by humanitarian crises.

Most neonatal deaths (75%) occur during the first week of life, and about 1 million newborns die within the first 24 hours. Among neonates, the leading causes of death include premature birth, birth complications (birth asphyxia/trauma), neonatal infections and congenital anomalies, which collectively account for almost 4 in every 10 deaths in children under 5 years of age
What was Sudan's neonatal mortality rate in 2023?
read.explanation: About 41,690 neonatal deaths a year. SuNAP aims for 50% of states to reach 12 or fewer neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births by 2030.

modules.title: Triage and Assessment of the Sick Newborn

sections.title: Triage of the newborn on arrival

read.text:
• Triage is a quick assessment and sorting process used to evaluate and categorize sick newborns shortly after they arrive at special care newborn units.
  • It helps prioritize care and treatment based on the severity of their condition and the available resources.
  • The healthcare provider should carry out a brief, focused assessment and categorize the newborn into one of the following three groups:
  • 1. Emergency Signs (Danger Signs)
These are indicators that the newborn is critically ill and at immediate risk of death if urgent intervention is not provided.
• 2. Priority Signs
These signs suggest that the baby requires prompt attention and should be moved ahead in the queue for timely assessment and treatment.
• 3. Non-Urgent Signs
These are signs that do not fall under emergency or priority categories and can wait for further evaluation without immediate risk.
The key signs indicating illness in newborns include:

• Poor feeding Decreased activity or altered consciousness
  • Fast breathing (over 60 breaths per minute)
  • Slow breathing (under 40 breaths per minute)
  • Chest indrawing
  • Grunting
  • Seizures
  • Bulging fontanelle
  • Evidence of circulatory impairment (Capillary Refill time ,BP, pulse rate/volume)
  • Floppiness or stiffness
  • Fever (above 37.5°C)
  • Hypothermia (below 36.5°C)
  • Discharge, bleeding, or redness around the umbilical area
  • More than 10 skin pustules or bullae, or any swelling, redness, or hardness of the skin
  • Pallor
  • Learning how to use thermometer ,check pallor ,
  • A video showing fast breath, slow breath, chest indrawing, seizures , postules and bullae

read.title: Signs of illness in newborns
read.caption: Fast and slow breathing, chest indrawing, grunting, seizures, pustules and bullae, pallor; using a thermometer.

read.text: Based on the presence or absence of these signs, newborns can be classified as normal, at risk, or sick. This classification supports timely prioritization and ensures appropriate, evidence-based care is provided promptly.
Newborns categorized as "Emergency" require immediate intervention and emergency care. These babies should be promptly stabilized and then admitted to the Special Newborn Care Unit (SNCU).
Those classified as "Priority" are ill and need a swift assessment followed by admission to the SNCU for appropriate care.
Newborns identified as "Non-Urgent" do not need immediate medical attention but still require a thorough evaluation and parental counseling.

modules.title: Welcoming and Admitting a Newborn to the Special Care Newborn Unit

sections.title: Admission to the SCNU: goals and the four steps

read.text: CONTENTS

• 1. Goals
  • 2. Introduction
  • 3. Importance
  • 4. Admission Process.
Goals

• 1. To ensure a high standard of neonatal care on admission at all levels if SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU)
  • 2. To minimize stress, conserving energy and time of the staff
  • 3. To enhance awareness and ensure readiness of SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) staff team for organized, and smooth admission process
Introduction

The admission process for a newborn to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU)) can be challenging and involves several key steps to ensure the baby's immediate stabilization and comprehensive care.
These steps need to be well organized, smooth and time effective aiming to increase Golden Hour success rates, decrease staff stress levels, and ultimately improve patient outcomes.
Importance
Admission of newborns, particularly sick newborns, is a crucial part of the Golden Hour of the baby life.
3.1 Admission process: welcoming
The steps of admitting a newborn to Special Care Newborn Unit (SCNU) can be looked at in the following order

• 1. Preparation before receiving the baby
  • 2. Receiving the baby Endorsement or handover Assessment Maintaining stability and Monitoring
  • 3. Writing and reviewing admission orders Sampling Procedures Medications
  • 4. Parental support

read.title: The four steps of admission, in order

steps.title: 1. Preparation before receiving the baby
steps.text: An admission team is organised as soon as the call comes; equipment checked; a warm environment.

steps.title: 2. Receiving the baby
steps.text: Endorsement or handover, assessment, maintaining stability and monitoring, done at the same time.

steps.title: 4. Parental support
steps.text: Updating, supporting and involving the parents.

sections.title: Preparing before the baby arrives

read.text: Immediately upon receiving a call or notification of an expected admission, an admission team is organized. The SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) team is multidisciplinary, including neonatologists/pediatrician, nurses, respiratory therapists ( if available), and other specialists, to provide comprehensive care. The SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) team prepares for the baby's arrival, including setting up necessary equipment and ensuring a warm environment. Equipment to be checked would include:

• a) Admission incubator/ warmer: (extreme preterm usually require special incubator), check if the incubator/ warmer is functioning, prewarm it, adjust temperature and humidity,
  • b) Admission trolley or cart: with all necessary supplies which are neatly organized and visible. Each compartment is labeled with the item name and quantity to make restocking easier. (like syringes, iv sets, iv fluids, gauzes, sample collection containers and other medications).
  • c) Vital signs monitor and its wires and connections.
  • d) Ventilatory support as recommended by the labour and delivery team. Nasal cannula, HHFNC, CPAP or Ventilator. Should be checked, ready and stand by.
  • e) Admission file with necessary charts like Ballard and growth parameters charts.
The call comes: a 28-week baby is on the way. Which of these does the manual list to check before the baby arrives?
options: Prewarmed incubator or warmer, admission trolley, vital signs monitor, the ventilatory support asked for, and the admission file
Only a cot and a blanket
read.explanation: Items a) to e) in "Preparation before receiving the baby".

sections.title: Receiving the baby: handover, assessment and stability

read.text: Once the baby arrived at SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) the next interventions had to be done simultaneously.

• a) Endorsement or handover:
    • A thorough handover from the transferring unit to the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) team is crucial, including details about the baby's condition, medications, and any special needs.
    • Each staff (medical and nursing staff) should receive their own endorsement.
    • Maternal, antenatal and perinatal history is reviewed and documented.
    • Admission orders should be reviewed carefully by the admission team
  • b) Assessment
    • Assessment, monitoring and maintenance of stability are ongoing processes during all steps of the golden hour of life.
    • A rapid assessment, including evaluation of vital signs (heart rate, breathing, admission temperature), a physical examination, and potentially some initial lab tests like blood gas analysis.
    • Growth parameters are measured immediately; however, the measurement may be delayed till the baby is stable enough.
    • A check list for endorsement and assessment would help organize the admission process and prevent confusion or missing important actions.
  • c) Maintaining stability and monitoring Once in the SCNU, the baby is closely monitored:
    • including vital signs, oxygen saturation, body temperature and other physiological parameters.
    • Maintenance of warmth to prevent serious hypothermia is crucial.
    • Incubator temperature (servo or manual) and humidity adjustment is very vital on admission.
    • Wrapping baby with plastic bags may needed especially extreme and VLBW infant
    • Degree of respiratory distress and efficacy of respiratory support should be monitored and adjusted as needed.
    • Blood glucose monitoring and judicious management of hypoglycemia is crucial to Prevent serious CNS complications of hypoglycemia.
On arrival, who receives the handover (endorsement)?
options: Each staff member, medical and nursing, receives their own
read.explanation: The manual: "Each staff (medical and nursing staff) should receive their own endorsement."

read.title: Receiving a newborn in the SCNU
read.caption: Three team members work at the same time on arrival: handover, rapid assessment and vital signs, warmth and monitoring; growth measurements when stable.

sections.title: Writing and reviewing admission orders

read.text: The most senior pediatrician/ neonatologist may need to give some verbal orders during assessment, however, the final admission orders should be written and recorded immediately after finishing the assessment. The orders should be very clear and in a systematic manner.

• a) Decide level of care
  • b) Systems:
  • CNS: sedation, imaging
  • CVS: monitoring, imaging, inotropes
  • Respiratory: type of support and settings of the machine, frequency of blood gases, imaging.
  • GIT: NPO vs feeding, imaging, NGT
  • Renal and fluid: TFI, type of IVF, UOP monitoring
  • Infectious diseases: cultures and antibiotics
  • Procedures: lines (UVC. UAC), LP, needle aspiration
  • Medications: antibiotics, others The orders must be recorded and reviewed by nursing staff (at least 2 nurses) and any confusion or unclear order should be clarified with the medical staff immediately. All requested blood samples should be withdrawn as soon as possible. IV medications are administered as soon as the IV line is ready. The nursing staff prepares for all procedures and assists the medical staff during procedures such as fixation of central lines.
Who reviews the written admission orders, and what happens to an unclear order?
options: At least 2 nurses review them; anything unclear is clarified with the medical staff immediately
The pharmacist at the end of the day
read.explanation: From "Writing and reviewing admission orders". The orders cover level of care and each system (CNS, CVS, respiratory, GIT, renal and fluid, infection, procedures, medications).

sections.title: Supporting the parents

read.text: The SCNU team provides ongoing support and education to parents, helping parents to understand their baby's condition and participate in their care

• The team updates the parents regarding the situation on admission and after stabilization, describe the acuity of the current condition and outline the management plan and expectations.
  • Parents should be supported and given the facts in a gentle way that consider their nature and respect their rights, beliefs and feelings. They should feel welcomed and be encouraged to visit their baby frequently.
  • A special team to support mothers for breast milk expression and breast feeding should always be available and ready to assist.
  • Parents will be asked to provide consent for any necessary procedures or treatments, including potential formula feeding if breastfeeding is not immediately feasible.
A father arrives in the SCNU an hour after admission. What does the manual say the team should tell and offer the parents?
read.answer: Update them on the situation on admission and after stabilization, describe how sick the baby is now, outline the plan and what to expect; give the facts gently, respecting their beliefs and feelings; welcome them to visit often; offer support for breast milk expression; ask consent for procedures and treatments.

sections.title: The golden hour, and keeping the baby warm in the SCNU

read.text: Goals

• 1. To understand the concept of Golden Hour
  • 2. To know the significance of Golden hour interventions
  • 3. To gain an approach that uses the best available evidence aiming to implement safe, effective and timely interventions
  • 4. Prevention of Hypothermia
  • 5. Support of Respiration
  • 6. Support of Cardiovascular System
  • 7. Support of Nutrition and hydration
  • 8. Prevention of Sepsis
Golden Hour Definition

Golden Hour of neonatal life is defined as the first hour of post-natal life in both preterm and term neonates. The Golden hour concept includes practicing all the evidence based intervention for term and preterm neonates, in the initial sixty minutes of postnatal life for better long-term outcome. Although the current evidence supports the concept of golden hour in preterm, still there is no evidence seeking the benefit of golden hour approach in term neonates,
Initial first hour of neonatal life includes

• 1. Early Essential newborn Care and neonatal resuscitation,
  • 2. post-resuscitation care,
  • 3. transportation of sick newborn to neonatal intensive care unit,
  • 4. respiratory and cardiovascular support and nutrition support
  • 5. initial course in SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU).
Importance of applying the Golden Hour concept and interventions

The neonatal management in the first hour of life have an important effect on both immediate and long-term outcomes of all neonates. The studies that evaluated the concept of golden hour in preterm neonates showed marked reduction in

• 1. hypothermia,
  • 2. hypoglycemia,
  • 3. intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH),
  • 4. bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), and
  • 5. retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).
What is the golden hour of neonatal life?
options: The first hour of postnatal life, in preterm and term neonates
read.explanation: Studies of the golden hour approach in preterm neonates showed marked reductions in hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, IVH, BPD and ROP.

read.text: 4.1 Prevention of hypothermia in special newborn care unit (beyond resuscitation)
The newborn body temperature should be kept within the neutral thermal zone during transport and on admission to SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) by maintaining between 36.7 and 37.2-degree C.
Any baby requiring humidity or with respiratory compromise or clinical instability should not be dressed or covered by fabrics.
All babies, irrespective of gestation, should have continuous skin temperature monitoring from admission until they are swaddled.

During resuscitations in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, it is essential to consider the maintenance of the newborn’s temperature. Cold stress may be eliminated by employing overhead heat on the resuscitative or ensuring appropriate heating in the incubator.
Between what temperatures is a baby kept during transport and on admission to the SCNU?
read.explanation: The manual: the neutral thermal zone, maintaining between 36.7 and 37.2 °C. Every baby has continuous skin temperature monitoring from admission until swaddled.

sections.title: Incubator, radiant warmer or cot?

read.text: Interventions in the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) that have been found to reduce hypothermia in very preterm infants include:

• use of servo-controlled incubators by targeting abdominal skin temperature set at 36.5° C
  • use of higher humidity compared to lower humidity in incubators.
  • use of topical emollients including coconut oil.
  • use of plastic wrap or plastic drapes for procedures in the special care newborn unit (SCNU).
  • use of kangaroo mother care for stable low birthweight infants.
Three main types of beds are used in the special care newborn unit (SCNU) is:

• 1. Incubators
  • 2. Open Care /Radiant Warmer
  • 3. Standard Cot
Incubators:

Are fully enclosed cots that allow heated air and humidity to be added to the baby’s environment whilst reducing stimuli including light and sound. These incubators are double walled to reduce radiant and conductive heat loss. Current incubators are efficient when only one side is opened for cares or procedures, but not when both sides are opened together which results in high convective and evaporative heat loss.

• All preterm infants ≤ 30 weeks’ gestation and / or ≤ 1000 g should be nursed in incubators.
  • Incubators are the admission bed of choice for all babies born < 33 weeks gestation or ≤ 1800 g.
  • Some preterm babies born ≥ 33 weeks’ gestation may require an incubator if hypothermic on admission.
  • Term and near-term infants may be swaddled and nursed in a cot if stable.
  • For those requiring respiratory care an open care system should be used.
  • Infants with suspected perinatal asphyxia should not be place in an incubator as this places them at risk of hyperthermia.
  • When using an incubator, avoid or minimize the time doors on opposite sides of the incubators are open during procedures and cares – this practice will increase heat loss via convention.
Open care/ Radiant warmers

• 1. Radiant Warmer, is a body warming device to provide heat to the body. They help to maintain the body temperature of the baby and limit the metabolism rate.
  • 2. The skin temperature of the baby can be monitored by a temperature measuring knob that is kept continuously attached to the body.
  • 3. Radiant Warmers can be manual or automatic (servo system – heater output is determined automatically based on skin temperature. The skin temperature is set at 36.5 degree Celsius) depending on the mechanism that the manufacturer employs for temperature control.
  • 4. The automatic model increases the heat output in small predetermined steps to reach at the desired temperature of the body.
  • 5. The device may seem simple to handle, but it is always recommended to have a proper training and read the manufacturers guidelines for person handling this equipments.
  • 6. It is necessary to regularly clean and disinfect the instrument.
  • 7. Generally, rdiant warmers result in increased IWL compared to incubators. This needs to be taken into account when calculating daily fluid requirements. ( A heat shield of thin polyethylene film can be used with a radiant warmer to reduce heat loss by convection and evaporation.
  • 8. The major advantage of the radiant warmer is the easy access it provides to critically-ill infants without disturbing the thermal environment. Its major disadvantage is the increase in insensible water loss produced by the radiant warmer. Most infants can be safely and adequately cared for in either incubator or radiant warmer bed.
Which bed does the manual say for each baby on admission?

items.text: A baby who needs respiratory care and easy access
A baby with suspected perinatal asphyxia (risk of hyperthermia in an incubator)

read.explanation: Incubators: all ≤ 30 weeks and/or ≤ 1000 g, and the admission bed of choice for < 33 weeks or ≤ 1800 g. Respiratory care: open care. Asphyxia: not in an incubator. Stable term: swaddled in a cot.

sections.title: The standard cot and moving a baby to a cot

read.text: Standard cot
Standard cots are opened beds used for:

• 1. Routine care for term and late preterm newborns in post- natal word and nursery
  • 2. Weaning preterm and sick babies from incubators or warmers
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Preparation for discharge. (see discharge process)
Each unite should specify its criteria for standard cot care.
Infant care post crib transfer

• Check temperature every hour x 4 after crib transfer. If temperature is between 36.2°C and 36.5°C, increase clothing layers if possible and add a pre-warmed blanket.
  • Continue to check temperature hourly until axillary temperature is ≥ 36.5°C for 4 consecutive hours.
  • If temperature is < 36.5°C for 3 consecutive hours (3 x hourly checks), return infant to a pre-warmed incubator.
Additional instructions

• BATHING should be deferred until temperature is maintained ≥ 36.5°C for a minimum of 12 hours after transition to crib.
  • Thereafter, normal unit bathing guidelines should be followed (e.g. CLABSI prevention strategies).
  • If infant has a central line (PICC), ensure site remains visible.
  • Infants with poor growth after transition may require return to an incubator due to increased energy expenditure maintaining thermal control.
After moving to a cot, the temperature is below 36.5 °C on 3 hourly checks in a row. What do you do?
options: Return the baby to a pre-warmed incubator
Bath the baby to warm him
read.explanation: From "Infant care post crib transfer". Bathing is deferred until the temperature has been ≥ 36.5 °C for at least 12 hours after the move to the cot.

sections.title: Supporting breathing after admission

read.text: Respiratory diseases are the leading cause of early neonatal morbidity and mortality, as well as the most frequent indication for both term and preterm neonates’ admission to the special care newborn unit (SCNU). The most common causes of admission to special care newborn unit (SCNU) are:

• Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) and prematurity.
  • Transient Tachypnea of newborn (TTN)
  • Congenital pneumonia
  • Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS)
  • Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH)
  • Tracheoesophageal Fistula
  • Congenital Heart Diseases
  • Metabolic disease.

The most common causes of admission in advanced SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) are RDS (preterm and extreme preterm babies) and TTN (late preterm and Term). According to currently available data, respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) affects about 80% of neonates born at 28 weeks GA, and this percentage increases to 90% at 24 weeks GA. About 50– 60% of these neonates need surfactant administration.
Modalities of respiratory support used in special care newborn unit (SCNU) and NICU: (see ventilation section)

• 1. Non-invasive Ventilation: (NIV)
    • a) nCPAP
    • b) Heated Humidified High Flow Nasal Cannula (HHHFNC)
    • c) Bi-PAP
    • d) NIVPP
    • e) Non-invasive neurally adjusted ventilator assist (NIV-NAVA)
    • f) Nasal high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (NHFOV)
  • 2. Invasive Ventilation (Mechanical Ventilation MV)
    • a) Conventional MV
    • b) High Frequency Ventilation (HHO and HFJ)

The type of respiratory support should be decided and SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) team informed before shifting the baby to SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU). (see Admission to SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) section)
What type of respiratory support?

• 1. Respiratory support of the critically ill neonate has steadily shifted from invasive to noninvasive forms of support.
  • 2. Mechanical ventilation (MV), although life-saving, is associated with chronic respiratory morbidity in both preterm and term born infants including bronchopulmonary Dysplasia BPD.
  • 3. New ventilation modes have been developed with the aim of minimizing lung injury. These include invasive and non-invasive respiratory support strategies and techniques for less invasive surfactant administration (LISA).
Non- invasive Ventilation (see Non-invasive Ventilation section) Nasal Continuous Positive Pressure nCPAP: can be applied as:

• A) Early CPAP: i.e. as a primary mode of ventilation started in the delivery room: now recommended as the optimal mode of respiratory support in infants at risk of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) who do not require intubation for stabilization). Systemic review showed that: Prophylactic or very early CPAP when compared to mechanical ventilation Reduced:
    • the incidence of BPD,
    • the combined outcome of death or BPD, and
    • mechanical ventilation.
  • B) Post Extubation CPAP (see Non-invasive Ventilation section).
Nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) (see Non-invasive Ventilation section)

• 1. NIPPV provides two levels of pressure:
    • a PEEP and
    • a PIP
  • 2. It is provided by a ventilator through a non-invasive interface (mask or prongs)
  • 3. can be synchronized with the infant's breathing. NIPPV vs CPAP: Early nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) in preterm infants at risk of respiratory distress within the first hours after birth reduced the
    • 1. risk of respiratory failure,
    • 2. the need for intubation,
    • 3. rates of treatment failure and
    • 4. mechanical ventilation
compared with early CPAP without increasing the risk of complications. (Cochrane review). Heated Humidified High Flow Nasal Cannula (HHHNC):

• 1. Flows of between 2 and 8 liters/ minute via nasal catheters
    • 2. Can be used as alternative of CPAP.
    • 3. Advantages: compared to CPAP:
      • perceived better access to the infant,
      • less nasal trauma and air leaks
      • quicker achievement of oral feeds
  • 4. Disadvantages
      • The pressure delivered to the lungs is unknown
      • Possible higher rate of treatment failure when used as primary mode.

sections.title: Surfactant

read.text: Surfactant Administration:

• 1. Surfactant administered in the delivery suite might prevent or reduce the severity of subsequent respiratory distress syndrome.
  • 2. From the available evidence the most effective way to optimize surfactant delivery and obtain a more homogeneous distribution of the drug is by using rapid bolus instillation in combination with appropriate alveolar recruitment techniques.
  • 3. The methods of surfactant administration (as well as ventilation strategies) are moving steadily from invasive (using ETT) to less invasive (no EETT) techniques.
  • 4. We will try to answer these questions
    • 1. Early vs Late surfactant?
    • 2. How to avoid intubation and mechanical ventilation aiming to reduce the rate of BPD without depriving some infants of the proven benefits of expedient provision of exogenous surfactant?
Methods of surfactant administration include

• 1. Using ETT
    • Prophylactic surfactant.
    • Early Rescue surfactant
    • INSURE technique
  • 2. Using a Special Catheter
    • Less Invasive Surfactant Administration (LISA) or Minimally Invasive Surfactant Therapy (MIST)
  • 3. Using Laryngeal Mask
    • Supraglottic airway (less invasive)
  • 4. Nebulized Surfactant Non-invasive
Prophylactic Surfactant:

Prophylactic use of surfactant refers to a strategy of providing exogenous surfactant at birth to infants at risk for RDS, with the aim of preventing severe RDS from developing. However, this strategy is NO longer indicated: Literature reviews showed:

• 1. With use of prophylactic surfactant there was trend toward increasing mortality, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) at 28 days and 36 weeks, and BPD or death at 36 weeks with the use of prophylactic surfactant. (level 1a evidence)
  • 2. Use of early CPAP or early non-invasive ventilation in the labour room was associated with:
      • a) tendency towards less BPD and mortality in preterm newborn.
      • b) Significant decrease in rate of intubation.
      • c) Significant decrease in need for surfactant administration.

However, infants with RDS who are already intubated during resuscitation should receive exogenous surfactant before inter-facility transport. Selective or Rescue surfactant Selective or rescue use of surfactant refers to a strategy of providing exogenous surfactant to infants with established RDS. It can be given early (less than 2 hours of age) or late (2 hours or beyond) Early versus delayed rescue surfactant

• 1. Early Rescue surfactant: administration of exogenous surfactant for preterm infants intubated for RDS within the first 2 h of age.
  • 2. Late Rescue surfactant: administration of exogenous surfactant for preterm infants intubated for RDS delayed until RDS was established, usually 2 h or beyond. Meta-analyses of six randomized trials showed that early surfactant was associated with a significant decrease in
      • mortality, BPD at 36 weeks,
      • BPD or death at 36 weeks, and
      • reduction in the risk of air leak,
      • with no increase in the risk for pulmonary hemorrhage or severe IVH.

What is the oxygen threshold for a baby on early CPAP to administer early rescue surfactant? A number of studies suggest that low (FiO2 0.30 to 0.50) versus high (FiO2 >0.55) thresholds show more benefit by providing surfactant earlier—before the development of more severe RDS—without increasing the rate of intubation significantly. In one systematic review published in 2007, analysis based on oxygen requirement criteria showed that a lower threshold (FiO2 ≤0.45) for intubation and surfactant administration was associated with less air leak and BPD compared with an FiO2 threshold >0.45. Two large randomized trials that did not allow infants initially managed with CPAP to receive surfactant until an FiO2 threshold of 0.6 was reached demonstrated higher rates of pneumothorax compared with those who were intubated and given surfactant early [24][32] (Level 1a evidence). Use of surfactant before inter-facility transport of preterm infants was found to be associated with lower oxygen requirement during transport and shorter duration of ventilation support, compared with controls [33] (Level 4 evidence).
What type of surfactant (synthetic vs animal derived: In summary animal-derived and the newer generation synthetic surfactants are both effective for

treating RDS and improving survival without BPD. When comparing different animal-derived surfactants, emerging evidence suggests that porcine minced lung extract, especially in higher dose, may be superior to bovine surfactant for improving acute respiratory status and reducing mortality or BPD in infants with RDS (Level 1a evidence)
(MCQs)
Which of the following is the correct indication for giving exogenous surfactant at birth under current recommendations?
options: A. All infants <32 weeks as prophylaxis
B. Any preterm infant on CPAP immediately after delivery
C. Infants already intubated during resuscitation with evidence of RDS
D. All infants with birth weight <1.5 kg
read.explanation: Correct answer: C

read.text: Prophylactic use of surfactant is no longer recommended in preterm infants primarily because of which of the following outcomes?
options: A. Significant reduction in BPD and mortality
B. Trend toward increasing mortality and BPD
C. No effect on intubation rates
D. Increased need for early CPAP
read.explanation: Correct answer: B

sections.title: Supporting and monitoring the circulation

read.text: The neonatologist should identify shock in compensated phase and should manage it aggressively.

• 1. The management includes
    • a) establishing early intravenous access,
    • b) judicious use of fluid resuscitation,
    • c) vasopressors (dopamine or ( or noradrenaline)) and
    • d) other supportive care like blood transfusion for hemorrhage, and antibiotics for septic shock
Monitoring support of CVS during the Golden hour after admission to SPECIAL CARE
NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU)

• 1. Clinical observation:
    • a) Heart rate
    • b) Pulse volume
    • c) Capillary refill
    • d) Markers of end-organ perfusion
  • 2. Non-invasive monitoring
    • a) Non-invasive arterial blood pressure measurement
    • b) Electrocardiogram
    • c) Echocardiogram
    • d) Pulse oximetry
    • e) Cerebral monitoring.
  • 3. Invasive monitoring
    • a) Intra- arterial BP monitoring
    • b) Arterial blood gas monitoring ( ABG)
    • c) Central venous pressure.
Clinical observations: This is the sim plest and most easily performed method

• a) Heart Rate:
    • 1. This is easily assessed at the bedside and requires no specialist equipment.
    • 2. An increased heart rate may reflect increased demand, for example hypovolemic states, seizures and the Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS).
    • 3. In the special care newborn unit (SCNU) setting however, other factors may result in tachycardia, such as agitation, pain and non-sinus arrhythmias.
  • b) Pulse Volume
    • 1. This is difficult to quantify on a clinical basis, but nevertheless is a useful method of assessment.
    • 2. A disparity between central pulses (palpable) and peripheral pulses (impalpable) usually indicates a cardiac problem or hypovolemia.
  • c) Capillary Refill Time (CRT)
    • 1. CRT has long been regarded as a quick and reproducible method of assessing circulatory status5.
    • 2. However, the traditional emphasis has been in the context of resuscitation rather than the post-resuscitation (ICU) phase, where doubts exist regarding its usefulness in reflecting CVS function. Markers of End- organ Perfusion:
    • 1. Skin color and temperature can be assessed quickly and may reflect the adequacy of the organ’s blood supply and therefore (indirectly) the patient’s cardiac output.
    • 2. However, their reliability in assessing cardiac function is low, especially in the ICU patient.

Non-invasive Monitoring

• a) Non-invasive blood pressure measurement NIBP:
    • 1. NIBP is widely used in all areas of health care.
    • 2. Measurement of systemic blood pressure (BP) is virtually universal and is vital in the assessment of organ perfusion.
    • 3. It is also an indicator of CO and systemic vascular resistance and therefore an important guide to therapy.
    • 4. The traditional method of using a mercury sphygmomanometer and stethoscope has been superceded by automated devices such as the Dinamap.
    • 5. In the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) setting, NIBP can be integrated into the overall monitoring system, allowing repeated estimations of NIBP at set intervals, the pressure is then displayed on the monitor screen alongside other parameters.
  • b) Electrocardiogram ECG:
    • 1. Continuous ECG monitoring is now ubiquitous in SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) and neonatal intensive care settings. It may be centralized (i.e. all patients’ ECGs displayed at a central monitor) or monitored at the bedside, or both.
    • 2. The ECG is primarily useful as an indication of heart rate, when peripheral perfusion is poor, for monitoring of bradycardia associated with apnoea and desaturations, and as an alert to the possibility of an arrhythmia. 3. Should an arrhythmia be suspected then a 12-lead ECG is mandatory.
  • c) Echocardiography
    • 1. The echocardiogram is a vital tool in assessment of cardiac function in the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU)
    • 2. It will provide information regarding cardiac size, preload, contractility and afterload which, together with heart rate, are the major factors that influence cardiac output.
    • 3. Its role has also been expanded to the neonatologist for rapid diagnosis of, for example, cardiac tamponade.
  • d) Pulse Oximetry:
  • 1. Pulse oximetry is a widely-used non-invasive technique but there are caveats to its use, for instance in a poorly- perfused extremity, anaemia or increased skin pigmentation.
  • 2. It cannot distinguish between carboxy- and oxyhaemoglobin and in methaemoglobinaemia the measurement is unreliable.
  • 3. The latest pulse oximeters aim to minimize the artifact that derives from patient movement.
  • e) Cerebral Monitoring:
    • 1. In neonates, alterations in the integrated electroencephalogram, monitored by a cerebral function monitor, may give the first indication of cardiovascular inadequacy.
    • 2. Near-infra-red spectroscopy (NIRS) is a global, non-invasive, continuous method of monitoring cerebral oxygen saturation.
    • 3. In practice a probe is applied to the skin (usually the forehead) which emits light, similar to a pulse oximetry probe.
    • 4. Its accuracy is heavily dependent on it distinguishing a signal from the brain rather than the intervening tissue (e.g. skin, muscle and bone)
    • 5. The tissue saturation derived is thought to be weighted to the greater proportion of venous blood in the area sampled.
    • 6. The readout is expressed as a percentage and the usual value is in the 60-80% range. Values lower than 42% are thought to indicate dangerous tissue hypoxia.

Near infra-red spectroscopy – The INVOS System uses two depths of light penetration to subtract out surface data, resulting in a regional oxygenation value for deeper tissues. Invasive cardiovascular monitoring

• a) Intra-arterial blood pressure (IABP)
    • 1. is a well-established method of monitoring a patient’s cardiovascular status.
    • 2. A pressure transducer measures the IABP and displays an arterial waveform via an intra-arterial cannula (commonly inserted in the radial, umbilical or posterior tibial artery).
    • 3. The cannula also allows regular sampling of intra-arterial blood for analysis.
    • 4. The arterial waveform may also be analyzed (pulse contour analysis) as it reflects the stroke volume and cardiac output, but must still be calibrated against CO measured by another method1
  • b) Arterial blood gas analysis:
    • 1. Analysis of blood obtained from an arterial source provides vital information regarding a patient’s cardiovascular status.
    • 2. Lactate ( part of ABG ) is produced at a cellular level as a result of anaerobic metabolism.
    • 3. Lactate is an important marker of cardiovascular function as an increase in blood lactate reflects tissue hypoxia.
    • 4. This may be as a result of low cardiac output or reduced tissue oxygen extraction1.
  • c) Central venous pressure
    • 1. Monitoring of CVP is more common in paediatric intensive care units and is rarely utilized in neonatal practice..

Summary of cardiovascular monitoring methods. ECG: Electrocardiogram; NIBP: Non-invasive blood pressure; IABP: Intra-arterial blood pressure; CRT: Capillary refill time; NIRS: Near-infra red spectroscopy; CVP: Central venous pressure.

sections.title: Nutrition: the stable term baby and the ten steps

read.text: Although, during the golden hour, the first priority and concerns are the ventilation, cardiorespiratory stability and prevention of hypothermia, a clear plan for support of nutrition should be the first priority after stabilization of the baby. The strategy and plan for nutritional support will depend on acuity of the babyś condition, the gestational age and whether there a special condition:

• 1. Stable term or preterm
  • 2. Preterm or sick newborn.

Overall, nutritional support in the delivery room and after SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) admission should be individualized and closely monitored to ensure adequate nourishment and metabolic stability for each newborn. Nutritional Requirements: Nutrient requirements include the following:

• Energy (measured as cal/kg/day)
  • Carbohydrates
  • Water
  • Minerals and trace elements
  • Protein
  • Vitamins
  • Fat
Support of nutrition of a stable term baby

The stable term or preterm who don’t have any contraindication of enteral feedings should be started on enteral feeds within golden hour with preference to mother milk or donor human milk Nutritional support in the delivery room should include prompt initiation of breastfeeding or provision of appropriate infant formula to ensure adequate nourishment for the newborn. Nutritional support for a stable newborn should prioritize prompt initiation of breastfeeding within half an hour of birth for stable term babies, following NRP and Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) guidelines. Breast feeding helps to reduce the risk of baby becoming ill in the first weeks and months of life.

Stable premature infants in the special care newborn unit (SCNU) are usually fed by OG or NG tube until they are sufficiently mature to coordinate sucking, swallowing, and breathing. Current evidence indicates that trophic or minimal enteral feedings are safe and well tolerated. In this technique, small volumes are fed to infants for a few days without significant increments. sections.title: Nutrition: the preterm and sick newborn, and fluids

read.text: Support of nutrition of Preterm and sick newborn

For preterm or unstable newborns, nutritional requirements should be carefully managed, taking into account gestational age and fluid needs. Feeding babies in the special care newborn unit (SCNU) is quite different from feeding healthy babies. When babies are sick or premature, 1. they are often not well enough to breastfeed or take a bottle.

• 2. Premature babies may not be able to suck effectively. Or
  • 3. their GI (gastrointestinal) tracts may not be mature enough to digest feedings.
  • 4. Babies who have unstable health are often unable to take regular feedings.
  • 5. Babies with umbilical catheters and those who need help breathing, such as with a mechanical ventilator, may not be able to be fed. (This is because of the risk of problems such as aspiration (breathing food into the lungs).
For most of admitted newborns are ELBW, VLBW, EGLAN or sick term neonates, immediate feeding cannot be started and they are usually kept NPO on admission.
A central venous access particularly umbilical venous catheter ( UVC ) should be secured in these newborn and intravenous fluids (IVF ) should be started at earliest to prevent hypoglycemia
Ideally for such babies total parenteral nutrition ( TPN ) should be initiated in the first hour of admission

Fluid requirement The fluid requirement of the newborn will depend upon the 1) gestational age, and 2) sensible/insensible water loss. The goal of fluid replacement is to provide adequate calories, protein, lipids; and compensate for the ongoing fluid losses. In newborn infants the starting fluid on day 1 for birth weight:

• < 1000 gram is 100-150 ml/kg/day,
  • 1000-1500 gram is 80-100 ml/kg/day
  • for > 1500 gram is 60-80 ml/kg/day.
The total fluid intake per day should be monitored according to

• 1. Daily weight
  • 2. Fluid balance
  • 3. Urine output (UOP)
  • 4. Serum sodium level (most sensitive): (Clinically: signs of dehydration are poor predictors; capillary fill time is useful.
  • 5. Hemodynamically significant PDA, proven NEC or CHD.
Serum sodium and fluid requirement:

• 1. Hyponatremia with weight loss suggests sodium depletion and needs sodium replacement.
  • 2. Hyponatremia with weight gain suggests dilutional hyponatremia and requires fluid restriction.
  • 3. Hypernatremia with weight loss suggests dehydration and management includes fluid correction over 48 hours.
  • 4. Hypernatremia with weight gain suggests salt and water load and needs fluid and sodium restriction

sections.title: Nutrition: glucose and energy

read.text: Fluid restriction

The results from various studies have shown that restricted water intake has a beneficial effect on the incidence of PDA, BPD, NEC and death. Glucose requirement and Risk of hypoglycemia After admission to the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU), nutritional support should be tailored to the specific needs of the infant, including monitoring blood sugar levels and providing appropriate glucose and fluid intake to maintain stable metabolic function.
For newborns at high risk for developing hypoglycemia, such as

• 1) premature,
  • 2) intrauterine growth restricted, or 3) sick infants, glucose levels should be monitored in the golden hour after birth. The goal is to keep glucose level 50 -110 mg/dl and hypoglycemia should be managed with feeding, or dextrose infusion. Glucose infusion rate (GIR) is calculated and infusion is started at GIR of 4-6 mg/kg/min in preterm and 6-8 mg/kg/min in term neonates and increased gradually to 12 mg/kg/ min) as per the clinic condition of the newborn and symptoms of hypoglycemia.

This calculation of GIR is a simple (unites mg/kg/min): GIR = IV Rate (mL/hr) X Dextrose Conc (g/dL) X 1000 (mg/g) Weight (kg) X 60 (min/hr) X 100 (mL/dL) where the dextrose concentration is expressed as a whole number, e.g. 5 or 10. Hyperglycemia should also be monitored and managed appropriately, with blood sugar levels checked regularly and insulin therapy initiated if necessary. Each neonatal unite should have clear guidelines for management of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia Additionally, careful attention should be paid to metabolic disorders such as galactosemia or disorders of fatty acid oxidation.
Energy needs
The exact energy needs of a given neonate depend on several factors, including

• gestational age,
  • postnatal age,
  • weight,
  • route of energy intake,
  • growth rate,
  • activity, and
  • thermal environment.

Infants who are ill or experiencing stressful situations (sepsis, surgery, BPD) have higher energy requirements. Infants who receive parenteral nutrition (TPN) need less energy for adequate growth because they do not need to absorb the provided nutrients and have no fecal losses. As a result, 70-90cal/kg/day with 3-3.5g/kg/day of protein may be adequate for growth. Protein is not an ideal source of energy; rather, it is provided as a building block for new tissue. If adequate non-protein calories are provided, the nitrogen balance in the infant is positive and the protein provided is used to build new tissue. Therefore, even if energy intake from protein is included in calculations of total energy intake, not all of the protein-derived calories are available for energy expenditure. The ideal energy ratio provides

• 65% of the energy as carbohydrates and
  • 35% as lipids.

Most infants need 100-120cal/kg/day for adequate growth. Some need up to 160-180cal/kg/day (eg, infants with BPD). The total energy needs of a growing, enterally fed premature infant without any acute illness are listed as follows: Resting expenditure - 50cal/kg/day Minimal activity - 4-5cal/kg/day Occasional cold stress - 10cal/kg/day Fecal loss (10-15% of intake) - 15cal/kg/day Growth (4.5 cal/g of growth) - 45cal/kg/day

read.question: A 2 kg baby is on 10% dextrose at 7.2 ml/hour. Using the manual's formula, what is the glucose infusion rate?
read.explanation: GIR = rate (ml/h) × concentration (g/dl) × 1000 ÷ (weight (kg) × 60 × 100) = 7.2 × 10 × 1000 ÷ (2 × 60 × 100) = 6 mg/kg/min. The manual starts preterms at 4–6 and term babies at 6–8 mg/kg/min.

read.text: Most infants need how many calories a day for adequate growth?
read.explanation: Some need up to 160–180 cal/kg/day, for example infants with BPD. On TPN, 70–90 cal/kg/day may be adequate.

sections.title: Nutrition: breast milk and parenteral nutrition

read.text: Total required to produce a 10g/day weight gain - 125cal/kg/day
Mature human milk is made up of

• 3%-5% fat,
  • 0.8%-0.0% protein,
  • 6.9%-7.2% carbohydrate calculated as lactose, and
  • 0.2% mineral constituents expressed as ash.

The energy content is 60-75 kcal/100ml. Protein content is considerably higher and carbohydrate content lower in colostrum than in mature milk Total Parenteral Nutrition Nutrient requirements include the:

• Energy (measured as cal/kg/day)
  • Carbohydrates
  • Water
  • Minerals and trace elements
  • Protein
  • Vitamins
  • Fat

Total parenteral nutrition (TPN ) should provide adequate nutritional requirements mentioned above. The American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (ASPEN) recommends parenteral nutrition (PN) be started within 24 to 48 hours of life for premature and VLBW neonates to promote growth and development while avoiding malnutrition and metabolic derangement. If patient-specific PN is not available immediately after birth, starter PN formulations may be used. The daily protein and lipid requirement in ELBW/VLBW neonates is around 4-4.5 gm/kg/day and 3 gm/kg/day respectively.. The content of a starter TPN usually include:

• dextrose,
  • lipids and
  • protein
  • NO electrolytes in starter TPN
When does ASPEN recommend starting parenteral nutrition for premature and VLBW neonates?
read.explanation: A starter PN (dextrose, lipids and protein, no electrolytes) can be used if patient-specific PN is not available.

read.text: Scenario:

A preterm newborn with birth weight 2 kg and poor feeding due to sepsis. He experienced frequent episodes of hypoglycemia ( RBG < 46mg/dl) and on dextrose infusion and imperial antibiotics pending culture results.
Calculate the glucose infusion rate according to the newborn requirement.
Work through the scenario using the manual: what GIR does a preterm start on, and how is it adjusted?
read.answer: The manual: start the infusion at a GIR of 4–6 mg/kg/min in preterm (6–8 in term) neonates and increase gradually, up to 12 mg/kg/min, according to the clinical condition and signs of hypoglycaemia; keep glucose at 50–110 mg/dl. For this 2 kg baby, 4–6 mg/kg/min of 10% dextrose is 4.8–7.2 ml/hour (rate = GIR × weight × 6 ÷ concentration). Discuss the exact plan with your facilitator.

sections.title: Prematurity: definitions and classification

read.text: Objectives

• 1. To strengthen the knowledge and focusing on premature newborn as a highly special population and distinct group of sick babies.
  • 2. To increase the awareness of complication of prematurity aiming for effective prevention and management.
  • 3. To develop an effective strategy for caring of preterm sick babies in SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) setup.
  • 4. To participate actively with strong base of knowledge aiming to reduce mortality and morbidity associated with prematurity.
  • 5. To strengthen the knowledge and focusing on premature newborn as a highly special population and distinct group of sick babies.
  • 6. To increase the awareness of complication of prematurity aiming for effective prevention and management.
  • 7. To develop an effective strategy for caring of preterm sick babies in SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) setup.
  • 8. To participate actively with strong base of knowledge aiming to reduce mortality and morbidity associated with prematurity.
5.1 Introduction to prematurity epidemiology
Definitions
Preterm babies are defined as babies born alive before 37 weeks of pregnancy are completed. Classification: There are sub-categories of preterm birth, based on gestational age:

• Extremely preterm: < 28 weeks.
  • Very preterm: 28 to 31 6/7 weeks.
  • Moderate to late preterm: 32 to < 36 6/7 weeks

Some references further classify extreme preterm babies born between 23 to 25 weeks as micro preemie. (however, birth wt should be less than 500grams). Another classification for preterm newborn is based on birth weight

• Low birth weight: less than (LBW) 2500 grans (between 1500 and 2500 grams.
  • Very LBW: 1000 to 1500 grams.
  • Extreme low birth weight: less than 1000 gram ( 500 to 1000 grams )
  • Micro preemie: less than 500 grams
Classify each baby by gestational age (the manual's sub-categories).
groups: Moderate to late preterm (32 to < 36 6/7 weeks)
read.explanation: By weight: LBW < 2500 g; very LBW 1000–1500 g; extremely LBW < 1000 g; micro preemie < 500 g.

read.text: Peri-viability (or limit of viability)

• Earliest stage of fetal maturity where there is a reasonable chance, although perhaps not a high likelihood, of extrauterine survival. This period is generally between 22 and <26 weeks gestational age (GA).
  • Most infants born at ≥26 weeks GA have a high likelihood of survival, whereas virtually none born at <22 weeks GA survive.
  • Clearly the “limit of viability” is a moving target: Shaeffer and Avery’s textbook, Diseases of the Newborn (1971), estimated the limit of viability to be around 28 weeks’ gestation and/or 1000 g.

sections.title: Prematurity: the burden and its challenges

read.text: Epidemiology

• Preterm birth complications are the leading cause of death among children under 5 years of age. Three-quarters of these deaths could be prevented with current, cost-effective interventions.
  • Across countries, the rate of preterm birth ranges from 4–16% of babies.
  • Approximately 900 000 children die in 2019 of complications of preterm birth.
  • Many survivors face a lifetime of disability, including learning disabilities and visual and hearing problems.
  • Inequalities in survival rates around the world are sharply clear.
  • In low-income settings, half of the babies born at or below 32 weeks (2 months early) die due to a lack of feasible, cost-effective care such as warmth, breastfeeding support and basic care for infections and breathing difficulties.
  • In high-income countries, almost all these babies survive.
  • Suboptimal use of technology in middle-income settings is causing an increased burden of disability among preterm babies who survive the neonatal period.
Mortality:

In the last 50 to 60 years the survival rates of premature infants substantially increased because of technological advances. Preterm births account for approximately 70% of neonatal deaths and 36% of infant deaths, as well as 25-50% of cases of long-term neurologic impairment in children. The mortality rate is high in developing countries, especially those of Sub-Saharan Africa. The perinatal mortality rate is 70 deaths per 1000 births; the neonatal mortality rate is 45 deaths per 1000 live births.

In 2023 the Sudan’s neonatal mortality rate (NMR) was estimated as 24.8 per 1,000 live births, translating to nearly 41,690 new-borns dying annually. The stillbirth rate is estimated to 21.51 deaths per 1,000 births translating into 36,973 annual deaths.
Prematurity challenges:

• Need for advanced respiratory support and care,
  • Maintenance of body temperature
  • hemodynamic stability,
  • Nutrition, feeding.
  • maintenance of growth as well as dealing with very delicate and sensitive immature organs.
Preterm births account for about what share of neonatal deaths?
read.explanation: The manual: preterm births account for approximately 70% of neonatal deaths and 36% of infant deaths. In low-income settings, half of babies born at or below 32 weeks die.

read.text: Morbidity and complications:

Premature infants are prone to have complications. These complications are gestational age dependent. Complications are inversely proportionate to gestational age. These complications can range from devastating intracranial hemorrhage, sepsis, severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia (chronic lung disease), and necrotizing enterocolitis totalis to minor feeding related issues.
Etiology of prematurity: Preterm delivery may be:

• 1. Indicated because of obstetric risks or complications
  • 2. Spontaneous because of preterm labor

sections.title: Why babies are born early: indicated and spontaneous preterm birth

read.text: indicated preterm delivery Obstetric risks or complications

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends late preterm delivery in conditions such as multiple gestation with complications, preeclampsia, placenta previa/ placenta accreta, and prolabor rupture of membranes.

ACOG recommends delivery as early as 32 weeks in selected cases involving multiple gestation with complications. Quasi-elective delivery earlier than 32 weeks is done on a case-by-case basis to manage severe maternal and/or fetal complications.
Spontaneous preterm delivery

In an individual patient, spontaneous preterm delivery may or may not have an obvious immediate trigger (e.g., infection, placental abruption). There are many risk factors: a-Past obstetric or gynecologic history:

• Prior preterm birth (highest risk)
  • Prior cervical conization procedure (cold knife cone or loop electrosurgical excision procedure)
  • Prior dilation and curettage procedure for spontaneous abortion or therapeutic abortion
  • Cervical insufficiency, cervical polyps, uterine fibroids, or maternal congenital reproductive tract abnormalities (e.g., bicornuate uterus)
  • Chronic diabetes
  • Hypertension
  • Kidney disease
b-Obstetric risk factors related to the current pregnancy:

• Short interpregnancy interval (< 6 months)
  • Extremes of pre-pregnancy weight (underweight or obese) or of weight gain during pregnancy (gaining more or less weight than recommended)
  • Pregnancy achieved by in vitro fertilization
  • Multiple gestation (e.g. twins, triplets)
  • Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy
  • Placental abruption or placenta previa
  • Preterm labor
  • Preeclampsia
  • Infections (e.g. bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, urinary tract infection, sexually transmitted infection, intra-amniotic infection)
  • Chronic diabetes or gestational diabetes
  • Pre-labor rupture of membranes
  • Little or no prenatal care
  • Certain congenital defects (fetuses with structural congenital heart defects are nearly twice as likely to be delivered prematurely as fetuses without congenital heart defects)
  • Multiple gestation is an important risk factor; 59% of twins and > 98% of higher-order multiples are delivered prematurely. Many of these infants are very preterm; 10.7% of twins, 37% of triplets, and > 80% of higher-order multiples are delivered at < 32 weeks of gestation.
c-Lifestyle or demographic risk factors:

• Younger or older maternal age (eg, < 16 years, > 35 years)
  • Non-Hispanic Black or American Indian/Alaska Native women (in the United States)
  • Undernutrition
  • Cigarette smoking
  • Use of alcohol or illicit drugs
  • Exposure to certain environmental pollutants
  • Domestic violence
  • Stress or lack of social support
  • Long work hours with long periods of standing
  • It is unclear how much risk some of these lifestyle or demographic risk factors contribute independent of their effect on other risk factors (eg, nutrition, access to medical care).
Which is the highest risk factor for spontaneous preterm delivery?
read.explanation: From "Spontaneous preterm delivery": prior preterm birth (highest risk). 59% of twins and > 98% of higher-order multiples are born preterm.

sections.title: Preventing preterm delivery

read.text:
• 1. PROGESTERONE THERAPY
    • In women with single gestation pregnancy and a history of spontaneous preterm delivery, antenatal progesterone therapy is the most effective strategy to decrease the risk of a recurrent preterm delivery. Progesterone supplementation is beneficial in these women starting at 16 to 24 weeks’ gestation and continuing through 34 weeks’ gestation.
    • women with no history of spontaneous preterm delivery if they have a cervical length of 20 mm or less before 24 weeks’ gestation.
    • Progesterone is not beneficial in multiple gestation pregnancies.
  • 2. CERVICAL CERCLAGE AND PESSARY
    • Studies have shown that cerclage is associated with a decrease in preterm delivery and in perinatal death when used in women with a prior preterm delivery and a cervical length of 25 mm or less.
    • The benefit of cerclage in women with a short cervix but no history of a preterm delivery is uncertain.
    • Cerclage is not recommended for multiple gestation pregnancies and has been associated with a twofold increased risk of preterm delivery (RR = 2.2; 95% CI, 1.2 to 4) in twin pregnancies.
  • 3. CORTICOSTEROID THERAPY
    • Once preterm labor is confirmed, a single course of corticosteroids is the only intervention for improving neonatal outcomes.
    • Betamethasone, two 12-mg doses given intramuscularly 24 hours apart, or dexamethasone, four 6-mg doses given intramuscularly every 12 hours, is recommended between 24 and 34 weeks’ gestation, and may be considered as early as 23 weeks’ gestation, in women likely to deliver within seven days regardless of membrane status.
    • The use of corticosteroids is associated with decreased neonatal morbidity and mortality.
    • Infants whose mothers receive antenatal corticosteroids are less likely to exhibit respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular hemorrhage, and necrotizing enterocolitis compared with those whose mothers did not receive corticosteroids.
    • Recent data suggest that a second rescue course of antenatal corticosteroids may be considered if the first dose was given more than seven days earlier and there is still a risk of preterm delivery before 34 weeks’ gestation.
    • 4. MAGNESIUM SULFATE
    • Because of its neuroprotective effect, administration of antenatal magnesium sulfate has been associated with a decrease in occurrence and severity of cerebral palsy in infants.
    • 5. TOCOLYSIS
    • The role of tocolytic /agents is to prolong the time to delivery so that antenatal corticosteroids and potentially magnesium sulfate can be administered, and the mother can be transferred to a tertiary care facility with a neonatal intensive care unit.
    • Tocolytics have not been shown to directly improve neonatal outcomes, and they are not always indicated.
    • First-line agents used to delay delivery up to 48 hours include calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine, nicardipine), beta-adrenergic receptor agonists (e.g., terbutaline), and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as prostaglandin inhibitors (e.g., indomethacin, ketorolac).
    • Magnesium sulfate can be used as a tocolytic but is associated with significant maternal adverse effects.
IMPORTANT

• must be used if combining magnesium sulfate with beta-adrenergic receptor agonists or calcium channel blockers because of possible maternal complications.
    • Contraindications to Tocolysis
      • Intrauterine fetal demise
      • Lethal fetal anomaly
      • Non reassuring fetal status
      • Severe preeclampsia or eclampsia
      • Maternal bleeding with hemodynamic instability
      • Chorioamnionitis
      • Preterm premature rupture of membranes*
      • Maternal contraindications to tocolysis (agent specific) *—In the absence of maternal infection, tocolytics may be considered for the purposes of maternal transport, steroid administration, or both.
  • 6. ANTIBIOTICS
    • Intrauterine bacterial infections are associated with preterm labor, especially before 32 weeks’ gestation.
    • Although several trials have been conducted, no studies have shown that use of antibiotics during preterm labor is effective in delaying delivery or reducing neonatal morbidity associated with preterm delivery.
Preterm labour is confirmed at 30 weeks. Which single intervention does the manual say improves neonatal outcomes?
options: A course of antenatal corticosteroids (e.g. betamethasone two 12 mg IM doses 24 hours apart)
read.explanation: Corticosteroids reduce RDS, IVH and NEC. Antenatal magnesium sulfate reduces cerebral palsy. Tocolytics have not been shown to improve neonatal outcomes directly.

sections.title: WHO recommendations: preventive care of the preterm baby

read.text:
1. Any KMC• Kangaroo mother care (KMC) is recommended as routine care for all preterm or low-birth-weight infants.
• KMC can be initiated in the health-care facility or at home and should be given for 8–24 hours per day (as many hours as possible).
2. Immediate KMC• Kangaroo mother care (KMC) for preterm or low-birth-weight infants should be started as soon as possible after birth
3. Mother’s own milk• Mother’s own milk is recommended for feeding of preterm or low-birth-weight (LBW) infants, including very preterm (< 1.5 kg) infants
4. Multicomponent fortification of human mil• Multicomponent fortification of human milk is not routinely recommended for all preterm or low-birth-weight (LBW) infants but may be considered for very preterm (< 32 weeks’ gestation) or very LBW (< 1.5 kg) infants who are fed mother’s own milk or donor human milk.
5. Preterm formula• When mother’s own milk and donor human milk are not available, nutrient- enriched preterm formula may be considered for very preterm (< 32 weeks’ gestation) or very low-birth-weight (< 1.5 kg) infants.
6. Early initiation of enteral feeding• Preterm and low-birth-weight (LBW) infants, including very preterm (< 32 weeks’ gestation) and very LBW (< 1.5 kg) infants, should be fed as early as possible from the first day after birth.
• Infants who are able to breastfeed should be put to the breast as soon as possible after birth.
• Infants who are unable to breastfeed should be given expressed mother’s own milk as soon as it becomes available.
• If mother’s own milk is not available, donor human milk should be given wherever possible.
7. Responsive and scheduled feeding• In health-care facilities, scheduled feeding may be considered rather than responsive feeding for preterm infants born before 34 weeks’ gestation, until the infant is discharged.

8. Fast and slow advancement of feeding• In preterm or low-birth-weight (LBW) infants, including very preterm (< 32 weeks’ gestation) or very LBW (< 1.5 kg) infants, who need to be fed by an alternative feeding method to breastfeeding (e.g. gastric tube feeding or cup feeding), feed volumes can be increased by up to 30 ml/kg per day.
9. Duration of exclusive breastfeeding• Preterm or low-birth-weight infants should be exclusively breastfed until 6 months of age
10. Iron supplementation• Enteral iron supplementation is recommended for human milk fed preterm or low-birth-weight infants who are not receiving iron from another source.
11. Zinc supplementation• Enteral zinc supplementation may be considered for human milk-fed preterm or low-birth-weight infants who are not receiving zinc from another source
12. Vitamin D supplementation• Enteral vitamin D supplementation may be considered for human milk-fed preterm or low-birth-weight infants who are not receiving vitamin D from another source
13. Vitamin A supplementation• Enteral vitamin A supplementation may be considered for human milk-fed very preterm (< 32 weeks’ gestation) or very low-birth-weight (< 1.5 kg) infants who are not receiving vitamin A from another source.
14. Probiotics• Probiotics may be considered for human-milk-fed very preterm infants (< 32 weeks’ gestation).
15. Emollients• Application of topical oil to the body of preterm or low-birthweight infants may be considered.

read.text:
1. Family involvementFamily involvement in the routine care of preterm or low- birthweight infants in health-care facilities is recommended.
2. Family support2. Family supportFamilies of preterm or low-birth-weight infants should be given extra support to care for their infants, starting in health-care facilities from birth and continued during follow-up postdischarge. The support may include education, counselling and discharge preparation from health workers, and peer support.

What are the four WHO recommendations on family involvement and support?

sections.title: Perinatal management: counselling, history and immediate care

read.text: Perinatal management plans should consider

• 1. Antenatal Counselling for premature labour
  • 2. History relevant to preterm delivery
  • 3. Decide the mode of delivery,
  • 4. use of intrapartum monitoring
  • 5. immediate care of the premature newborn
      • promote optimal respiratory functioning, maintain a neutral thermal environment, prevent or reduce risk of potential complications, and maintain homeostasis.
      • Starting to early feeding, especially with breast milk, is crucial for the infants. It is also crucial for those who are not breastfeeding, rather whose needs are maintained by a healthcare team. These specially trained people are the newborn nurses who have a key responsibility on infant feeding as a result of their dense interactions with the infants and mothers from the beginning. To be able to fulfill this role, nurses need to know enteral feeding techniques and the nursing care of the enterally fed infants.
      • Whenever possible, extreme preterm birth should be managed in a maternity facility co-located with a designated neonatal intensive care unit.
      • Risk assessment should be performed with the aim of stratifying the risk of a poor outcome into three groups: extremely high risk, high risk and moderate risk.
      • If life-sustaining treatment for the baby is anticipated, pregnancy and delivery should be managed with the aim of optimizing the baby’s condition at birth and subsequently.
  • 6. Family councils
      • Parents should be supported throughout and encouraged to seek advice and further support from others, such as family members and religious advisers
  • a. Antenatal Counselling for premature labour

Antenatal counselling should be provided by senior neonatologists, obstetricians, and midwives Management decisions should depend on what the parents and their medical advisers think is in the child’s best interests Parents should have accurate information on likely outcomes for their infant—including their chances of survival and the risk of longer term disability Information on outcomes provided to parents should cite data from large cohort studies that reported the outcome of all pregnancies for each week of gestation (not just for infants admitted to intensive care units)

• Antenatal counselling should be provided by senior neonatologists, obstetricians, and midwives
  • Management decisions should depend on what the parents and their medical advisers think is in the child’s best interests
  • Parents should have accurate information on likely outcomes for their infant— including their chances of survival and the risk of longer term disability
  • Information on outcomes provided to parents should cite data from large cohort studies that reported the outcome of all pregnancies for each week of gestation (not just for infants admitted to intensive care units)
  • Perinatal management plans should consider the mode of delivery, use of intrapartum monitoring, and immediate care of the newborn
  • Decisions not to provide active resuscitation or intensive care should not be binding, particularly if the newborn seems more mature than anticipated
  • It may be appropriate to provide full resuscitation and intensive care to infants at birth until the clinical progress becomes clearer and further discussions with the family have been possible
  • Parents should be supported throughout and encouraged to seek advice and further support from others, such as family members and religious advisers
  • Infants who are not actively resuscitated or in whom active resuscitation is withdrawn should receive
  • palliative care

• b. History relevant to preterm delivery
  • Maternal medical and obstetric history: (Last menstrual period, Fetal ultrasonography (based on the first fetal ultrasound in early pregnancy).
  • Estimated gestation
  • Singleton or multifetal pregnancy
  • Assessments of fetal growth and wellbeing
  • Details of suspected congenital anomalies
  • Risk of fetal-maternal infection and chorioamnionitis
  • Course of labour, if labouring
  • Intrapartum monitoring results
  • Antenatal interventions, tocolytic drugs, steroids, antibiotics
  • Use of opiates and an aesthetic drug
  • c. Immediate care of the preterm infant:
Preparing appropriately for the delivery and immediate care of the preterm infant is essential when time permits and may impact on the eventual outcome for the premature infant.

• The level of resuscitation that may be needed is inversely related to the gestation of the preterm infant.
  • Usually, preration taken in resuscitating preterm infants of > 32 completed weeks’ gestation is the same as that taken for term infants. Most need only basic measures such as drying and stimulation.
  • Infants of gestation < 32 weeks (or birth weight< 1500 g) require more active support.
  • For infants of < 28weeks’ gestation, this support will probably include endotracheal intubation and assisted ventilation.
  • Ideally, two members of staff who are experienced in the early care of preterm infants should be present at the delivery of each anticipated infant.
  • Before delivery, the attending staff should recheck essential equipment for resuscitation.
A baby of 34 weeks is about to be born. What does the manual say about resuscitation?
options: Above 32 weeks it is the same as for term infants; most need only drying and stimulation
Only babies < 34 weeks need a team
read.explanation: Below 32 weeks (or < 1500 g) more active support is needed; below 28 weeks this probably includes intubation. Ideally two experienced staff attend each anticipated preterm delivery.

sections.title: Resuscitation equipment, the limit of viability and palliative care

read.text: Equipment for resuscitation of the preterm infant

• Clock with second hand
  • Dry, warmed towels and heat source
  • Light source
  • Wide bore suction device
  • Facemasks in a variety of sizes
  • Inflatable bag with blow-off valve
  • Oxygen source with pressure limiting device
  • Laryngoscope with neonatal blades
  • Endotracheal tube (sizes 2.5, 3.0, and 3.5)
  • Needles and syringes
  • Umbilical catheters
Infants born at the threshold of viability

• Although interventions (such as prophylactic antenatal steroids and exogenous surfactants) have improved certain outcomes for extremely preterm infants, recent data indicate that the overall prognosis for infants born at < 26 weeks’ gestation remains poor.
  • When delivery at < 26 weeks’ gestation is anticipated, the most experienced paediatrician available must counsel the parents and inform them of the potential outcomes for mother and infant.
  • If possible, the parents should then be allowed to reflect on the implications of this information before it is decided how to care for the newborn infant.
Palliative care of the newborn infant

• If resuscitation is unsuccessful, or if active resuscitation is felt to be inappropriate, then palliative care should be provided for the infant and family.
    • The parents can spend time with their baby and should be aware that their baby may show signs of life, such as occasional gasps, after birth.
    • Privacy and sensitive support for parents and family with subsequent follow up are essential.
    • Factors needed in the palliative care of extremely preterm infants
        • Warmth
        • Dignity
        • Human contact
        • Pain relief
  • d. postnatal physical parameters
    • After delivery, newborn physical examination findings also allow clinicians to estimate gestational age, which can be confirmed by the new Ballard score.
    • Reflexes develop at different times during gestation. The Moro reflex begins by 28 to 32 weeks of gestation and is well established by 37 weeks. The palmar reflex starts at 28 weeks and is well established by 32 weeks. The tonic neck reflex starts at 35 weeks and is most prominent at 1 month post term.

read.title: Palliative care of the extremely preterm baby: what is needed

read.text: Estimate Gestational age using new bellard score:

• Obtain a gestational age score on all babies weighing less than 2000g, within 24 hours of
  • delivery. This assists in making appropriate care plans, especially at the limits of viability. It is preferable to wait until baby is “settled” before scoring, but sometimes an early score (soon after delivery) is essential.
  • Score for both neuromuscular and external/physical features. Add each to give a final score, and then give a maturity rating (in weeks) by referring to the conversion table. Complete the process by plotting baby’s weight and length on the neonatal growth chart, and documenting whether baby is appropriate, under- or overweight for gestational age.
Neuromuscular maturity sign

Assess all six features with baby lying supine (spine on bed), and awake but not crying. Refer to the chart while assessing. Accuracy is improved if you assess both sides of the body, and use the average score.

• 1. Posture: Observe the posture. Handling the infant may improve the assessment
  • 2. Square Window: Flex the hand at the wrist. Exert pressure sufficient to get as much flexion as possible. The angle between the hypothenar eminence and the anterior aspect of the forearm is measured and scored.
  • 3. Arm Recoil: Fully flex the forearms with the hands at the shoulders for 5 seconds, then fully extend by pulling the hands. Release as soon as the elbows are fully extended, and observe the recoil (degree of flexion at the elbows).

sections.title: New Ballard score: physical maturity; monitoring and screening

read.text: Physical Maturity

• 1. Skin: Examine the skin over the front of the chest and abdomen, and also look at the limbs. More mature infants have thicker skins.
  • 2. Lanugo: This is the fine, fluffy hair that is seen over the back of small infants. Except for very immature infants that have no lanugo, preterm infants have a lot of lanugos and this decreases with maturity. The infant has to be turned over to examine the amount of lanugo on the back. If the infant is too sick to be turned over, then the amount of lanugo is not scored.
  • 3. Plantar creases: Use your thumbs to stretch the skin on the bottom of the infant’s foot. Only note definite creases and not very fine wrinkles that disappear when the skin is stretched. More mature infants have more creases. To measure the length of the foot in very small infants place a measuring tape on the sole and measure the distance in mm from the back of the heel to the tip of the big toe.
  • 4. Breast: Both the appearance of the breast and the size of the breast bud are considered. Palpate for the breast bud by gently feeling under the nipple with your index finger and thumb. More mature infants have a bigger areola and breast bud.

• 5. Ears and eyes: Both the shape and thickness of the external ear are considered. With increasing maturity, the edge of the ear curls in. In addition, the cartilage in the ear thickens with maturity so that the ear springs back into the normal position after it is folded against the infant’s head. The eyelids separate with increasing maturity.
  • 6. Genitalia: Male and female genitalia are scored differently. With maturity the testes descend in the male and the scrotum becomes wrinkled. In females the labia majora increase in size with maturity

Weight should be assessed daily if tolerated;
