      • b. appropriate testing for any identified problems or disorders,
      • 1. Hematologic abnormalities: Complete blood count (CBC), reticulocyte count, and differential count are done initially and at intervals to detect common abnormalities
      • 2. electrolytes balance: Serum electrolytes, glucose, calcium, and phosphate levels need to be periodically measured, particularly in infants receiving parenteral fluids and/or nutrition (e.g., very preterm and extremely preterm infants), and during the diuresis seen in the first days of life.
      • 3. bilirubin level: Transcutaneous and/or serum bilirubin levels are measured to detect and monitor this disorder.
      • 4. Systemic infection: CBC with manual differential, C-reactive protein, blood culture, and sometimes procalcitonin levels are often done to facilitate early detection of neonatal sepsis
      • 5. Central nervous system infection: Lumbar puncture is typically reserved for infants with clear signs of infection and/or seizures, a positive blood culture, or an infection that is not responding to antibiotics
      • 6. serum calcium, alkaline phosphatase, and phosphorus levels (to screen for osteopenia of prematurity), X-rays, often obtained for other reasons, may provide evidence of osteopenia and/or unsuspected fractures. DXA scanning and quantitative ultrasonography scanning may detect osteopenia but are not in widespread use.
      • 7. hearing evaluation,
      • 8. cranial ultrasonography to screen for intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia, in Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), Screening cranial ultrasonography is indicated at 7 to 10 days in preterm infants < 32 weeks and in older preterm infants with complex courses (e.g., known IVH, cardiorespiratory and/or metabolic instability). Intraventricular hemorrhage in extremely preterm infants may be clinically silent, and a routine cranial ultrasound is recommended for these infants. The incidence of IVH decreases with increasing gestational age, so routine screening of preterm infants > 32 weeks is not considered useful unless they had significant complications.
      • 9. As with older neonates, routine newborn screening tests are done at 24 to 48 hours of age.

Screening for retinopathy of prematurity is recommended for infants born ≤ 1500 g or ≤ 30 weeks of gestational age and for larger and more mature infants who have had an unstable clinical course. The first examination is done according to a schedule based on the infant's gestational age (see table Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity). Examinations are usually repeated at 1- to 3-week intervals depending on the initial findings and are continued until the retina is mature. Some of these follow-up examinations are done after the infant is discharged. The use of digital photographic retinal images is an alternate method of examination and follow-up in areas where a skilled examiner is not routinely available.

sections.title: Necrotising enterocolitis: stages, risk factors and differential diagnosis

read.text: Necrotizing Enterocolitis:

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a devastating disease that affects mostly the intestine of premature infants. itis an Acute inflammatory disease in newborn intestine characterised by hemorrhagic necrosis, which may lead to perforation and destruction of the gut. Clinical presentation usually comprises triad of abdominal distension, gastrointestinal bleeding and pneumatosis intestinalis (air in bowel wall on abdominal X-ray) Modified Bell’s criteria
Stage 1: Suspected NEC : clinical signs suggestive but X-ray non-diagnostic

• a. Systemic signs: nonspecific symptoms
  • b. Intestinal signs:
  • a. increased gastric residuals
  • b. abdominal distension
  • c. vomiting
  • d. blood in stools
  • c. Radiological signs:
  • a. normal/mild intestinal dilatation
  • b. thickened bowel loops Stage 2: Definite NEC: mild-to-moderately ill, abdominal X-ray demonstrates pneumatosis intestinalis and/or gas in biliary tract
  • a. Systemic signs: see Stage 1 +/- mild metabolic acidosis, mild thrombocytopenia, raised CRP
  • b. Intestinal signs: see Stage 1 + absent bowel sounds, +/- localised abdominal tenderness, abdominal cellulitis or right lower quadrant mass, bright red blood and/or mucus from rectum (exclude local pathology)
  • c. Radiological signs: significant intestinal dilatation, pneumatosis intestinalis, portal vein gas, +/- ascites, persistently abnormal gas pattern (e.g. localised dilated loop of bowel seen on serial X-rays or gasless abdomen)
Stage 3: Advanced NEC: severely ill, bowel intact or perforated

• a. Systemic signs: see Stage 2 + hypotension, bradycardia, severe apnoea, combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis, DIC, neutropenia
  • b. Intestinal signs: see Stage 2 + signs of generalised peritonitis, marked tenderness, distension of abdomen
  • c. Radiological signs: see Stage 2 + pneumoperitoneum +/- ascites
Risk factors

• Prematurity
  • Intrauterine growth restriction
  • Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow on umbilical arterial Doppler antenatally
  • Perinatal asphyxia
  • Low systemic blood flow during neonatal period (including duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
  • Significant patent ductus arteriosus
  • Exchange transfusion
  • Formula milk
  • No antenatal corticosteroids
  • Infections with: Klebsiella, Enterobacter, anaerobes
Differential diagnosis

• Sepsis with ileus
  • Bowel obstruction
  • Volvulus
  • Malrotation
  • Spontaneous intestinal perforation:
  • associated with early postnatal corticosteroids or indomethacin
  • abdominal X-ray demonstrates pneumoperitoneum but does not show evidence of pneumatosis intestinalis Systemic candidiasis:
  • clinical signs can mimic NEC with abdominal distension, metabolic disturbances, hypotension and thrombocytopenia
  • Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES)
  • usually preceded by thrombocytosis in association with formula milk
  • take thorough feeding history, and establish any temporal relationships with type of feed

read.text: INVESTIGATIONS

• A. Abdominal X-ray : Supine antero-posterior view, If perforation suspected but not clear on supine view, left lateral view , Not all babies will have radiological findings associated with NEC (Stage 1)
  • B. Blood tests
  • 1. FBC: anemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia often present; early return to normal.
  • 2. Blood film: evidence of hemolysis and toxic changes (e.g. spherocytes, vacuolation and toxic granulation of neutrophils, cell fragments, polychromatic cells)
  • 3. CRP, but a normal value not informative in initial phase
  • 4. U&E
  • 5. Blood gas: evidence of metabolic acidosis (base deficit worse than -10), raised lactate
  • 6. Coagulation screen
  • 7. Blood cultures
IMMEDIATE TREATMENT

• 1. Always discuss management with consultant neonatologist In all stages
  • 2. Nil-by-mouth
  • 3. Transfer baby to neonatal intensive care and nurse in incubator
  • 4. If respiratory failure and worsening acidosis, intubate and ventilate
  • 5. Gastric decompression
  • 6. Free drainage with large NGT (size 8)
  • 7. NEC often associated with significant third space fluid loss into peritoneum
  • 8. Triple antibiotics: flucloxacillin, gentamicin and metronidazole
  • 9. IV fluids/PN: total volume ≤150 mL/kg
  • 10. Long line when stable and bacteraemia/septicaemia excluded
  • 11. Pain relief, consider morphine/diamorphine infusionStage 2: Proven NEC (confirmed radiologically)
  • 12. If breathing supported by nasal CPAP, elective intubation to provide bowel decompression (see Intubation section)
  • 13. Give IV fluid resuscitation sodium chloride 0.9% 10 mL/kg for shock and repeat as necessary. Shock is
  • 14. most common cause of hypotension in babies with NEC.
  • 15. If coagulation abnormal, give FFP
  • 16. If thrombocytopenia and/or anaemia occur, transfuse
  • 17. Discuss with surgical team: may need transfer to surgical center

In recovery phase

sections.title: Intraventricular haemorrhage: signs and ultrasound screening

read.text: the symptoms of intraventricular hemorrhage
IVH is often asymptomatic but the likelihood of signs increases with the severity of hemorrhage. The following are the most common symptoms of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH):

• Apnea and bradycardia (stopping breathing and low heart rate)
  • Pale or blue coloring (cyanosis)
  • Weak suck
  • High-pitched cry
  • Seizures
  • Swelling or bulging of the fontanelles
  • Anemia
Diagnosis of intraventricular hemorrhage:

• a complete medical history
  • a physical examination,
  • Ultrasound Screening
Ultrasound screening 1st Ultrasound

• The first ultrasound should routinely be performed between days 5 and 7 of life.
  • This is the optimal time for a single ultrasound examination as all cases of IVH and >90% of associated parenchymal haemorrhages will be evident .
  • However, as many haemorrhages occur on the first day of life and the vast majority by 48 hours earlier ultrasound examination may be performed on the basis of clinical concerns or as part of the ongoing research of the unit.
2nd Ultrasound

• The second cranial ultrasound should routinely be performed around day 28 of life. By this stage parenchymal abnormalities and\or ventriculomegaly will be evident, providing important prognostic information and guidelines for further management.
Additional ultrasound scans are indicated in the following circumstances:

• Infants >29 weeks gestation in whom there are clinical concerns or who are considered to be at significant risk (see risk factors).
  • Head circumference growth deviating from the normal intrauterine growth curves. This situation is most common after Grade III-IV IVH and is indicative of progressive hydrocephalus.
  • Ventriculomegaly on the routine day 28 scan
When is the first routine cranial ultrasound done in this lesson, and the second?
read.explanation: Days 5–7 catch all IVH and > 90% of parenchymal haemorrhages; day 28 shows parenchymal changes and ventriculomegaly.

sections.title: Preventing IVH; apnoea of prematurity

read.text: Prevention of intraventricular Hemorrhage Antenatal Interventions

• The administration of antenatal corticosteroids to the mother 48 hours prior to delivery significantly reduces the incidence of IVH and should be considered for all women at risk of preterm delivery.
  • Maternal magnesium sulphate Observational studies have described a reduced incidence of IVH in the preterm infants of women exposed to intravenous magnesium sulphate but not all studies support this.
  • Management of preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) with antimicrobial therapy in the expectant management of preterm premature rupture of the membranes is associated with a significant reduction in the number of women who deliver within one week and a reduction in chorioamnionitis, neonatal sepsis and IVH.
Treatment for intraventricular hemorrhage: There is no specific treatment for IVH. Sometimes, surgery is necessary to stabilize the condition of the baby.
Apnea of Prematurity
Absence of breathing in the premature infant for a period of > 15 seconds often associated with bradycardia and/or hypoxia. Epidemiology

• Recurrent prolonged apnea and bradycardia occurs in most infants under 30 weeks gestation, in about 50% of infants at 30-32 weeks gestation, and only about 10% of those at 34-36 weeks gestation.
  • The more premature the infant, the greater the possibility of apnea occurring. Apnea of prematurity is primarily due to immaturity of the respiratory center and control of the upper airway; most cases are due to a combination of central and obstructive apnea.
  • It is important to manage the following additional factors which can either cause or accentuate apnea:
    • Systemic illness - sepsis, hypoxemia, shock.
    • CNS – IVH, seizures, asphyxia, cerebral malformations.
    • CVS conditions: e.g. PDA
    • Anemia
    • Drugs - opiates, sedation.
    • Post-general anesthesia.
    • Metabolic disturbances: hypoglycaemia, hypocalcemia, inborn error of metabolism.
    • Hypothermia, hyperthermia.
    • Obstructive respiratory problems - macroglossia, micrognathia, tracheomalacia,
    • choanal atresia
    • Gastro-esophageal reflux.
Management

• Address any underlying factor that may be aggravating apnoeic episodes.
  • Monitor infants with cardio-respiratory monitoring and oxygen saturation. Refer to Monitoring and Observation Frequency.
  • If an episode of apnea/bradycardia does not resolve spontaneously, gentle tactile stimulation maybe required. If response is slow or cyanosis present then bag and mask ventilation may be needed.
  • Prone positioning stabilizes the chest wall, reducing the frequency of apnea.
  • CPAP should be optimized. Occasionally non-invasive ventilation (NIPPV) may be required. Intubation is sometimes required when the above fails.
  • Caffeine is a potent cardiac, respiratory and CNS stimulant and is the pharmacological agent of choice. It has been shown to decrease apnea and reduce the need for ventilator support. It also reduces short term morbidities such as BPD and ROP, is cost-effective and improves long term outcomes with lower rates of developmental co-ordination disorder. For dosage and side effects refer to Neonatal Medication Protocols - Caffeine.
Who to Treat

• Infants < 30 weeks gestation are generally prescribed caffeine routinely. Caffeine has been shown to reduce post-extubation apnea.
  • Infants 30-34 weeks gestation are generally prescribed caffeine if they are symptomatic.
  • Consider prescribing caffeine for a neonate in the immediate post-operative period following a general anesthetic, or prior to immunizations in an ex-preterm neonate.
Which babies are generally given caffeine routinely?
read.explanation: Infants 30–34 weeks are generally given caffeine if symptomatic. Apnoea of prematurity: > 15 seconds of no breathing, often with bradycardia and/or hypoxia.

sections.title: Stopping caffeine; respiratory distress in the late preterm

read.text: Stopping Caffeine

• There are no trial data to support decisions to cease treatment.
  • Apnea of prematurity decreases with advancing age and can generally be expected to resolve by 37 weeks corrected gestational age (CGA). Apnea which continues beyond this period is often multifactorial.
  • Caffeine can generally be ceased between 32- & 34-weeks’ gestation, provided the baby has been stable. Some extremely preterm neonates will require treatment for longer.
  • Once the infant has ceased caffeine, infants should remain monitored with an oximeter for a minimum of 5 days and for 48 hours after the last apnoea/bradycardia. Refer to Monitoring and Observation Frequency. In general we do not measure caffeine levels routinely.
  • Consider measuring caffeine levels:
    • To check therapeutic levels if there are ongoing symptoms.
    • If there is concern that caffeine levels may be too high (signs may include persistent tachycardia).
Respiratory Distress

• The late preterm infant is at high risk for respiratory distress within the first few hours of birth. Multiple studies have found that late-preterm infants are at
  • increased risk for respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN), pneumonia, and air leaks (pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum) requiring respiratory support with the rate of respiratory
  • complications steadily decreasing with each increasing week in gestational age.
  • Many late preterm infants are delivered by Caesarean section, which also increases the risk.
  • Antepartum steroids have been found to decrease the risk.
  • Observe preterm for nasal flaring, tachypnoea, grunting, sternal recessions and cyanosis Parameters, including respiratory rate, heart rate and temperature should be documented every 3 hours for the first 12 hours at least, A respiratory rate persistently more than 60/min is abnormal.
  • Oxygen saturations should be measured if the infant has any signs of respiratory distress and a medical assessment performed.
  • Saturations must be measured from the right upper limb (preductal) using an appropriate oxygen probe and monitor with the probe shielded from ambient light.
  • Infants who develop persistent respiratory distress (e.g. tachypnoea, grunting or a persistent requirement for supplemental oxygen) should be transferred to NICU for further management
  • Respiratory distress can be the result of other conditions such as hypoglycaemia
  • Any infant showing respiratory distress should not be allowed to feed orally. If feeds are ordered they should be via a nasal gastric tube
  • To confirm the diagnosis, the medical team may want to take X-rays of the premature baby’s chest.
  • An X-ray of a preemie with RDS will likely show:
Xray finding

• small lung volume
  • air bronchograms or air in the airways of the lung that are black in comparison to the surrounding white areas that do not contain air
  • granular-looking areas on the lung where the lung resembles white salt and black pepper being sprinkled on the film. The more pepper, the more aeration; the more salt, the more collapse or fluid.
  • In suspected cases of RDS, X-rays are not always taken immediately because sometimes the baby needs to be placed on a ventilator urgently. The chest X-ray is taken after the baby has been stabilized on the ventilator.
Where is the oxygen saturation of a late preterm with respiratory distress measured?
options: The right upper limb (preductal), probe shielded from light

sections.title: Jaundice: physiological or pathological?

read.text: Jaundice :
More than 50% of normal newborns and 80% of preterm infants have some jaundice.
Jaundice may be normal or abnormal
Causes of Neonatal Jaundice
Physiological Jaundice : Appears after 24 hours, peaks at day 3–5, resolves by 1–2 weeks.

Pathological Jaundice : Jaundice that appears within 24 hours, is excessively high, rises rapidly, lasting > 14 days in term and > 21 days in preterm infant, mainly due to Increased Bilirubin Production (Haemolysis)

• Haemolytic disease of the newborn (blood group incompatibility)
  • Red cell enzyme defects
  • Red cell membrane defects
  • Sepsis with haemolysis
other causes

• glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
  • congenital syphilis or other intrauterine infection
  • liver disease such as hepatitis or biliary atresia (stools pale and urine dark)
  • hypothyroidism
IMPORTANT Red Flags for Pathological Jaundice

• Onset <24 hrs.
  • Bilirubin rises >5 mg/dL (85 µmol/L) per day.
  • Total serum bilirubin > 17 mg/dL (290 µmol/L) in a term infant OR > 15 mg/dL (255 µmol/L) in the first 48 hours.
  • Jaundice lasting >2 weeks (unconjugated) or >3 weeks (conjugated).
  • Conjugated bilirubin >20% of total.

Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is an irreversible but preventable leading cause of childhood and lifelong visual disability.

Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), first known as "retrolental fibroplasia," is a major blinding disease among children in the United States (US). Thus far, 3 "epidemics" of ROP-induced blindness have been reported. The first epidemic was seen in the 1940s and 1950s in developed countries, most commonly associated with unregulated supplementary oxygen. After regulating and monitoring at birth of high oxygen (ROP virtually disappeared) the survival rates of preterm infants at ever-earlier gestational age, to eventually also lower birth weights with re-emergence of ROP as a major problem is chronicled in the second epidemic that started in industrialised countries from 1970s. Finally in the mid-1990s, the third epidemic began in low- and middle-income nations (first in Eastern Europe and Latin America, expanding to East and South Asia and finally to sub-Saharan Africa) due to both high rates of preterm delivery and varied levels of new-born care in these countries. Some countries or regions within countries lack the equipment and resources to optimise their care, and typically ROP is detected in larger and older new-borns exposed to unregulated oxygen (similar to what had occurred in the US decades earlier).

sections.title: Retinopathy of prematurity: cause and prevention

read.text: Etiology:

In utero, the fetus is in a hypoxic state. When infants are born prematurely, the relative oxygen level is sometimes increased even when oxygenation is at ambient levels. High supplemental oxygen can be damaging to capillaries.

The cause of ROP is premature birth and additional factors that cause a mismatch between normal retinal vascularization and the oxygen need of the developing retina. There is also consideration of maternal factors affecting nutrition and inflammation/infection.

ROP is a dynamic pathology, does not presented at birth, but after 2-3 weeks, for this the parents should be worn about the risk of developing ROP in their preterm baby. So, the early retinal examination should be in NICU or immediately after discharge, then repeat the fundus examination after 3-4 weeks searching for signs of progression or regression of the condition,
ROP visual loss control strategies:
It requires efficient collaboration within different specialties (Obstetrician, midwife, Neonatologist, ophthalmologist).
Primary Measures:

• follow up of preterm deliveries.
  • antenatal steroid for threatened preterm deliveries.
  • in-suite transfer for an equipped facility with NICU for threatened preterm deliveries.
  • delayed umbilical cord clamping (ideally after 60 to 90 seconds),
  • promoting kangaroo care.
  • Early provision of breast milk,
  • gentle resuscitation-use CPAP.
  • avoid 100% unmonitored O2 supplement-use oximeters, and use oximeters and set saturation target and alarm).
  • prevent sepsis (good hygiene, aseptic techniques)
  • promote breast feeding.
  • avoid blood transfusion (consult neonatologist).
Which of these is a primary measure to prevent ROP?
options: Avoid 100% unmonitored oxygen: use oximeters with saturation targets and alarms
Give oxygen at 100% to all preterms
read.explanation: ROP is not present at birth but appears after 2–3 weeks; first examination at about 4 weeks postnatal age.

read.text: Secondary Measures:

• 1st or 2nd indirect ophthalmoscopy at 4 weeks postnatal age.
  • Repeat in 1 or 2 weeks depending on retinal vascularization.
  • early detection, classification, and timely management of sight threatening-ROP.
  • If Type 1 ROP or plus disease suspected, refer to tertiary centers.

read.text: Tertiary measures:

• confirm the diagnosis.
  • treatment protocole (laser photocoagulation, Intravitreal anti-VEGF, of complex retinal surgery)
  • follow-up regularlly until regreeion or advancement of the condition.

Contributing risk factors:

  • 2. Induced pregnancy.

read.text: KMC definition

Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is an evidence-based method of care for premature and low-birth-weight infants (specifically those birth weight less than 2 kg ) that involves skin-to-skin contact with the mother (or father or caregiver) and exclusive and frequent breastfeeding.
Importance and benefits:
KMC regulates baby’s temperature, heart rate, breathing and oxygen saturation, reduces incidence of apnoea and bradycardia and associated with better neurodevelopment
6.1 KMC indication and Contraindication
indications:
Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is indicated for neonates who are preterm and/or have low birth weight, specifically those with birth weight less than 2,000 grams.
contraindications:

• Major congenital malformation
  • Ongoing seizure activity
  • Sever jaundice requiring immediate management (e.g. exchange transfusion)
  • Life threatening instability
  • Inability of parent or caregiver to provide KMC (including medical or psychological or social reason or refusal to consent

read.text: Discuss benefits of kangaroo care for both parents and baby at any available opportunity
Daily shower or washing is sufficient for maternal/ parental hygiene;

read.text: Contents:

Goals:

  • 3. Improve the safety of using medication.
9.1 Patient Safety Introduction:

Background: Ensuring patient safety is a global necessity focused on averting medical errors that could lead to fatalities, injuries, or harm. It has become a fundamental component of neonatal care. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), medical errors affect 1 in 10 patients globally, with potential consequences such as death, lasting or temporary harm, financial setbacks, and psychosocial distress for both the patient and, in certain instances, the caregiver. The distinctive characteristics and complicated nature of the neonatal intensive care unit (SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU)) environment, coupled with the heightened vulnerability of the neonatal population, amplify the likelihood of medical errors, Consequently Clear and efficient communication among healthcare team members is essential for patient safety, where even minor errors can lead to severe and life-threatening outcomes. Definition: Patient safety is defined as freedom from accidental injury. Ensuring patient safety involves the establishment of operational systems and processes that minimise the likelihood of errors and maximise the likelihood of intercepting them when they occur. Importance:

Over the past decade, there has been significant attention directed towards patient safety concerns, particularly following the publication of the IOM report 1999. This focus has led to the introduction of numerous patient safety initiatives, statements, goals, and campaigns by various professional organizations, regulatory bodies, and accrediting agencies. Key among these initiatives are The Joint Commission National Safety Goals, the Institute of Health Improvement's 100,000 Lives Campaign, and the Safety and Quality Improvement Act of 2005.

According to the IOM Report of 2001, healthcare providers are urged to provide care that is effective, evidence-based, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable. Moreover, the report emphasizes that patients should not experience harm as a result of the care they receive.
Objective: By the end of this section the candidate should be able to:

• 1. Enhance Patient Safety through Improved Recognition of Standards for Patient Identification and Verification.
  • 2. Optimize Medication Safety Protocols for Patient Well-being.
  • 3. Strengthen Communication Effectiveness for Enhanced Patient Care.
How does the manual define patient safety?
read.explanation: WHO: medical errors affect 1 in 10 patients globally. The SCNU environment and the vulnerability of newborns amplify the risk.

sections.title: Identifying the right baby

read.text: Patient identification regarding newborns is very important as they are a vulnerable population at high risk for misidentification; many reasons for this as they were all born with similar birth dates and similar medical records numbers, multiple will have identical surnames, and be hospitalized at the same time, additionally they are unable to talk to confirm their identity and lack the distinguishing physical attributes and characteristics that are specific to the adult population. A considerable risk is related to patient misidentification resulting in many errors, including:

• Providing two vaccines to the same infant.
  • The wrong infant being circumcised.
  • Feeding a mother's expressed breastmilk to the wrong newborn.
  • Giving a breastfed infant formula or a mother breastfeeding the wrong infant.
  • Hospitals caring for newborns will be required to use at least two patient identifiers when providing care, treatment, and services to newborn infants.
Examples of methods to prevent misidentification may include the following:

• 1. Distinct naming systems could include using the mother’s first and last names and the newborn’s gender (for example: “Smith, Judy Girl”; or “Smith, Judy Girl A” and “Smith, Judy Girl B” for multiples).
  • 2. Standardized practices for identification banding (for example, two body-site identification and barcoding) and the medical record number to be added in the two bands.
  • 3. Establish communication tools among staff (for example, visually alerting staff with signage noting newborns with similar names).
For pediatric and neonatal patients, use the methods described below to ensure that patients are correctly identified before taking blood.

• Use a wrist or foot band only if it is attached to the patient; DO NOT use the bed number or a wristband that is attached to the bed or cot.
  • If a parent or legal guardian is present, ask that person for the child's first and last name.
  • Check that the name, date of birth, and hospital or file number are written on the laboratory form, and match them to the patient.
  • verbal / telephone order/ closed loop order

options: Use at least two identifiers from a band attached to the baby; never the bed number or a band on the cot

sections.title: Clear communication

read.text: Clear communication between healthcare team members in the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) is an essential component of patient safety, where small errors and misunderstandings could lead to serious harm or life-threatening conditions. Communication failures within healthcare systems are one of the leading causes of inadvertent patient harm, and having all team members on the same page has been shown to decrease adverse events. Consequently, the communication in the patient or plan of care must be actively-written, and the care providers should read back their verbal medical orders for verification and all written orders must contain standard acronyms and abbreviations throughout the organization. Enhancing communication and safety in the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU):

Another evening meeting to coordinate overnight issues.

sections.title: Prescribing and giving medicines safely

read.text: Often, medical errors are related to medication administration, Medication errors occur mostly in premature infants weighing less than 1500 grams on account of their need for more medical support including pharmacological measures. Errors in administering enteral nutrition and medications account for 13.3 percent of potentially harmful SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) errors. All prescriptions in neonatal patients require specific calculations and need to change when the newborn gets weight. According to Kaushal and colleagues, three-fourths of neonatal medication errors occur during the prescribing stage, The contents in the dead space of the hub of a needle and syringe may be enough to overdose a premature neonate. Despite a national patient safety goal-directed at patient identification, patient misidentification is common when administering drugs. Serious medication errors involving patient misidentification in the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) have ranged from 11 to 25 percent of reported adverse events. Identification in the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) is challenging when there are multiple gestation births and poor neonatal identification systems (such as identification bands that fall off). Ulrich and colleagues identified three environmental factors involved in increasing the likelihood of medication errors: under-illumination of the medication preparation area, distractions, and interruptions while handling medications. Improve the safety of using medication:

• Creating a routine preadministration process before giving any medication.
  • Double-checking of medications, including checking for the right patient, right drug, right dose, right time, and right route before administration.
  • replacing concentrated stock medications on the unit with a single dose system and increasing the number of personnel who must check medication for accuracy can be useful in decreasing the chance of errors.
  • Increasing the number of personnel involved can also increase the risk of error if it is assumed that someone else has already checked.
  • Availability of clinical pharmacists in monitoring orders.
  • use of information technology for example the integration of the computerized physician order entry (CPOE) in the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU), the use of barcoding devices, robots to dispense medication, and computerized medication administration records.
  • Critical incident analysis with a thorough examination of the event should be conducted when an event happens and a conclusion must be based on data and fact, not assumption. lessons must then be disseminated to be a preventive value.
  • other strategies could be the development of a SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU)-specific formulary and the use of emergency medication sheets listing calculated doses by weight.
At which stage do three-quarters of neonatal medication errors occur?
read.explanation: Kaushal and colleagues, in the manual. Double-check the right patient, drug, dose, time and route before every medicine.

sections.title: The neonatal sepsis surveillance system

read.text: Introduction:

Hospitalized new-borns are more vulnerable to healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), which are linked to higher mortality, duration of stay, and healthcare expenses, as well as the risk of neurodevelopmental impairment among survivors.
The optimization of infection prevention and control (IPC) techniques in special care Newborn Unit (SCNU) necessitates careful evaluation of the distinct population and environment.

Neonate sepsis still of leading cause of deaths among neonates, there is available accurate estimate of it burden, but major risk factors are existed, contribute to more frequent cases and complexity of purpose solutions.

read.note: Pre-test: answer these 10 questions before you start this module. You will take the same test at the end.

read.text: 10.1 Neonatal Sepsis Surveillance System
Surveillance System for the Neonatal sepsis is essential to monitor and prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and ensure the health and safety of new-borns.

Aim to systematically detect, report, and analyze cases of neonatal sepsis in order to guide prevention, control, and quality improved interventions to contribute in reduction of neonatal morbidity and mortality.
This system is designed to survey sepsis (blood stream infection), among preterm and sick neonates admitted to Sudanese pediatrics and obstetrics hospitals NICU.

It targeting all neonates born inside or outside hospitals, whatever their clinical cause of admission. it works on identifying cases of sepsis clinically or laboratory confirm by collecting appropriate clinical sample (blood, CSF, swab).
Specific objectives:

• Monitor the incidence and prevalence of neonatal sepsis.
  • Identify risk factors associated with Neonatal sepsis
  • Detect antimicrobial sensitivity and resistance patterns.
  • Evaluate the effectiveness of IPC interventions.
  • Provide data for benchmarking and quality improvement in neonatal care.
  • Facilitate timely response to outbreaks or clusters of neonatal infections.
Which of these is a specific objective of the sepsis surveillance system?
options: Detect antimicrobial sensitivity and resistance patterns
read.explanation: Also: incidence and prevalence, risk factors, IPC effectiveness, benchmarking, and timely response to outbreaks.

sections.title: Suspected sepsis: the signs and maternal risk factors

read.text: WHO defines suspected sepsis in a hospitalized infant aged 0–59 days as the presence of one or more of the following clinical signs:

• 1. Not feeding well or not able to feed at all
  • 2. movement only when stimulated or no movement at all
  • 3. high body temperature (≥ 38 °C)
  • 4. low body temperature (< 35.5 °C)
  • 5. severe chest indrawing
  • 6. convulsions

sections.title: Sepsis case definitions: clinical and laboratory-confirmed sepsis

read.text:
• 1. Absence of positive microbiological blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid culture AND
  • 2. Treatment with FIVE or more days of intravenous antibiotics was initiated AND
  • 3. Patient has at least TWO of the following clinical or laboratory features of generalized infection:
      • CNS manifestations: Convulsion, bulging fontanel, Irritability, lethargy, apathy
      • GIT manifestations: Refusal of feeding, feeding intolerance, abdominal distension or ileus
      • Unexplained temperature instability or fever (>38 °C) or hypothermia (<36.5 °C)
      • Unexplained tachycardia (>160/min) or bradycardia episodes (<100/min)
      • Capillary refill time of > 3 seconds or skin mottling
      • New/more frequent episodes of apnea (>20s)
      • Local infection (umbilical discharge – eye discharge)
      • At least one of the following laboratory findings:
        • Platelet count of less than (100 × 10³/µL)
        • WBC less than (4 × 103/µL) or more than (20 × 103/µL)
        • CRP (> 1 mg/dL)
        • Hyperglycemia (> 140 mg/dl) or Hypoglycaemia (< 46 mg/dl)
Laboratory Confirmed Neonatal Sepsis by a recognized pathogen
Recognized pathogen is recovered from a blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid culture Gram-Positive Bacteria

• Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)
  • Group B Streptococcus (GBS)
  • Streptococcus pneumonia
  • Enterococcus faecalis / Enterococcus faecium (including VRE)
  • Beta-hemolytic streptococci (Groups A, C, F, G)
  • Listeria monocytogenes – especially in early-onset sepsis
Gram-Negative Bacteria

• Escherichia coli – most common in early- and late-onset neonatal sepsis
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae
  • Enterobacter cloacae
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Serratia marcescens
  • Acinetobacter baumannii
  • Citrobacter spp.
  • Proteus spp.
Laboratory Confirmed Neonatal Sepsis by common commensals
If blood cultures show growth of one or multiple common commensals (e.g., coagulase-negative staphylococci)

• 1. A common commensal is recovered from TWO blood culture and/or CSF culture specimen AND
  • 2. Patient has at least TWO of the following clinical or laboratory features of generalized infection:
      • CNS manifestations: Convulsion, bulging fontanel, Irritability, lethargy, apathy
      • GIT manifestations: Refusal of feeding, feeding intolerance, abdominal distension or ileus
      • Unexplained temperature instability or fever (>38 °C) or hypothermia (<36.5 °C)
      • Unexplained tachycardia (>160/min) or bradycardia episodes (<100/min)
      • Capillary refill time of > 3 seconds or skin mottling
      • New/more frequent episodes of apnea (>20s)
      • Local infection (umbilical discharge – eye discharge)
      • At least one of the following laboratory findings:
        • Platelet count of less than (100 × 10³/µL)
        • WBC less than (4 × 103/µL) or more than (20 × 103/µL)
        • CRP (> 1 mg/dL)
        • Hyperglycemia (> 140 mg/dl) or Hypoglycaemia (< 46 mg/dl)
One blood culture grows coagulase-negative staphylococcus. Is this laboratory-confirmed sepsis?
options: Not on its own: a common commensal must grow from TWO cultures, with at least two clinical or lab features
Yes, if the baby is preterm
Only if the CRP is normal
read.explanation: From "Laboratory confirmed neonatal sepsis by common commensals". A recognised pathogen (e.g. E. coli, GBS) from one culture is enough.

sections.title: Treating neonatal sepsis

read.text:
• Start: Ampicillin + Gentamycin for 3 days awaiting culture results
  • If no growth repeat CRP/PCT: If negative and clinically stable STOP antibiotics.
  • Otherwise continue ampicillin IM/IV 50 mg/kg every 12 hours in the first week of life and every 8 hours after the first week of life for a total of at least 10 days plus gentamicin IM/IV 5 mg/kg once a day in the first week of life and 7.5 mg/kg once a day after the first week of life for a total of at least 10 days.
  • If culture positive, continue as indicated for at least 10 days
  • Alternative; Third-generation cephalosporins for a total of 2–17 days, but no or trivial difference.
  • Fungal prophylaxis has shown to cause significant reduction in incidence of invasive fungal infection in very preterm or VLBW infants. All ELBW/VLBW neonates can be started on fluconazole prophylaxis within golden hour provided the incidence of fungal sepsis is significant in the neonatal care unit (>5% at baseline). and European guide- lines suggest that 2% incidence of fungal sepsis should be the threshold).
  • Congenital infection at time of birth (viral infection like TORCH) should be treated promptly during the golden hour of life. Management consideration
  • Antibiotic stewardship limits the development of antimicrobial-resistant organisms and it can be done by improving use of antibiotics. Narrow spectrum antibiotics should be used, fixed protocols should be there for starting and stopping antibiotics, start antibiotic only when clinically indicated and downgrade antibiotics after seeing blood culture sensitivity pattern are few components of anti- biotic stewardship.
  • There is high risk of development of antibiotic resistance with the widespread use of antibiotics thus making careful and selective use of antibiotics to the highest risk patients a universal goal.
  • decision should also take into consideration local antibiotic resistance patterns

sections.title: Preventing sepsis: hand hygiene

read.text:
• Many interventions are done to prevent neonatal sepsis, but the most important are the standard infection control precautions, mainly hand washing and using asepsis precautions while handling the newborn
  • The newborn should be handled with strict asepsis techniques starting from the time the neonatal birth. All invasive procedures like umbilical line or peripheral cannula insertion, administration of surfactant, preparation of IV fluids, TPN, and antibiotics should be done using aseptic precautions and bundle approach should be used.
  • A clear written policy for infection control should be maintained and strictly implemented during all SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) procedure.
  • do not wear artificial fingernails or extenders when having direct contact with patients and natural nails should be kept short (≤ 0.5 cm long or approximately ¼ inch long).
Sepsis prevention and control interventions:

• 1. Hand hygiene
  • 2. Personal protective equipment (PPE)
  • 3. Safe injections and sharps injury prevention
  • 4. Environmental cleaning
  • 5. Appropriate handling and transport of linen
  • 6. Waste management
  • 7. Decontamination and reprocessing of reusable patient care items and equipment
  • 8. Aseptic technique
Hand hygiene

• Health workers should perform hand hygiene the right way and at the right time, as described below.
  • It is also important to take care of the hands by regularly using a protective hand cream or lotion, at least daily
  • If available, perform handrubbing with an alcohol-based handrub product as the preferred method for hand hygiene in health care, if hands are not visibly soiled
  • Apply enough alcohol-based handrub product to cover all areas of the hands; rub hands until dry (20–30 seconds).
  • Perform handwashing with soap and water if hands are visibly soiled. Wet hands and apply soap; rub all surfaces (40–60 seconds); rinse hands and dry thoroughly with a single-use towel; use the towel to turn off the faucet/ tap
Hands are not visibly soiled. What is the preferred hand hygiene, and for how long?
read.explanation: Visibly soiled hands: soap and water, 40–60 seconds, dry with a single-use towel and use it to turn off the tap.

sections.title: Preventing sepsis: personal protective equipment

read.text: Personal protective equipment
Use personal protective equipment (PPE) correctly

• ASSESS THE RISK of exposure BEFORE any health care activity.
  • Follow infection prevention guidelines.
  • Select PPE based on your assessment and the task.
      • Correct gloves (Clean, non-sterile)
      • fluid-resistant gown
      • Mask and eye protection or face shield
  • Perform hand hygiene before putting on and after taking off PPE.
What measures protect against respiratory infections? Precautions for everyone everyday

• Coughing or sneezing into a bent elbow or a tissue and disposing of the tissue immediately
  • Cleaning hands with alcohol-based hand rub or soap and water
Precautions for patients with respiratory infections

• Good respiratory hygiene, including wearing a medical mask
  • Prevention of droplet and/or aerosol transmission
  • Routine cleaning and disinfection of surfaces in mother and baby’s zone
  • Hand washing before and after breastfeeding
Wear gloves
Health workers should:

• wear gloves during activities that may involve exposure to blood and other body fluids.
  • the same pair of gloves should not be worn for the care of more than one patient
  • change gloves between tasks and procedures if moving from a contaminated body site to another body site on the same patient
Before any care activity, how do you choose PPE?
options: Assess the risk of exposure first, then select gloves, gown, mask or eye protection for the task
Wear nothing unless the baby is infected
Wear the same gloves all shift
read.explanation: Hand hygiene before putting on and after taking off PPE.

sections.title: Preventing sepsis: using gloves correctly

read.text: IMPORTANT

• that wearing gloves is not a substitute for hand hygiene
    • wear sterile gloves for aseptic procedures, such as surgery or catheter insertion
    • Incorrect glove use can result in infections and infections can kill.
    • reuse gloves after reprocessing or decontamination is not recommended.
    • Gloves do NOT protect against needle-stick or other puncture wounds. .Do not place used gloves on tables; dispose of them immediately in designated bins •
When do you put ON gloves?

• Before a sterile procedure
  • When anticipating contact with blood or another body fluid, regardless of the existence of sterile conditions, including contact with non-intact skin or mucous membrane
  • Before contact with a patient (and his/her immediate surroundings)
When do you take OFF gloves?

• As soon as gloves are damaged (or loss of integrity is suspected)
  • When contact with blood, another body fluid, non-intact skin or mucous membrane occurred and has now ended
  • When contact with a single patient and his/her surroundings or a patient’s contaminated body site has ended
  • When there is an indication for hand hygiene
examples of unsafe glove use

• Using gloves to replace hand hygiene
  • Wearing the same pair of gloves between patients
  • Washing gloved hands
  • reuse gloves after reprocessing or decontamination, as this is not recommended.
When do you take OFF gloves?
options: As soon as they are damaged, when contact with body fluid has ended, when care of one baby has ended, or when hand hygiene is indicated
Only at the end of the shift
read.explanation: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene, and do not protect against needle-stick injuries.

sections.title: Preventing sepsis: safe injections, cleaning, linen and waste

read.text: Safe injections and sharps injury prevention Health workers should:
• prepare injections in a clean workspace, where there is low risk of
contamination from blood, body fluid, splashes or sprays.

• perform hand hygiene prior to preparing the medication and touching the patient;
  • use a sterile, safety-engineered syringe;
  • use a sterile medication vial and diluent
  • always use a sterile syringe and needle to withdraw and reconstitute medications, and never leave a needle in the septum of a vial
  • avoid use of multi-dose vials or, if used, dedicate the vial for single-patient use.
  • label the multi-dose vial with the date opened, and discard according to the manufacturer’s instructions, when sterility is compromised or after 28 days.
  • clean the patient’s skin with soap and water or disinfect with 60–70% alcohol prior to the procedure
  • provide a puncture-resistant sharps container for sharps disposal at the point of care.
  • not re-cap, bend, break, manipulate or manually remove the needle from the syringe.
  • discard the sharps container when it is three quarters full, seal it and store it in a secure area
Environmental cleaning : Health workers should:

clean and disinfect patient care areas at least once a day, paying particular attention to frequently touched surfaces deal with spills of blood and body fluid/ substance as soon as possible, in accordance with local protocols.
Appropriate handling and transport of linen : Health workers should:

handle soiled linen and waste carefully (with minimal manipulation or agitation) to prevent personal contamination and transfer to other patients. remove heavily soiled material (e.g. faeces) from linen, while wearing appropriate PPE, before placing it in the laundry bag; store clean linen in a manner that protects it from environmental contaminants.
Waste management: Health workers should:

• treat waste contaminated with blood, body fluids, secretions and excretions as hazardous infectious waste, in accordance with local regulations.
  • treat human tissue and laboratory waste that is directly associated with specimen processing as hazardous infectious waste.
  • minimize the amount of waste produced by the healthcare facility.
Aseptic technique Health workers should:

• use sterile items and equipment for all aseptic procedures.
  • use aseptic technique for insertion and maintenance of all invasive devices and aseptic/clean clinical procedures for surgical procedures, wound dressing and similar, to prevent infections
Decontamination and reprocessing of reusable patient care items and equipment : Health workers should:

• handle equipment soiled with blood, body fluids, secretions and excretions in a manner that prevents skin and mucous membrane exposure, contamination of clothing and transfer of pathogens to other patients, or the environment.
  • clean and disinfect (or sterilize, depending on the type and use of patient care equipment) reusable equipment before use with another patients.
  • discard single-use devices after each use.
  • clean and disinfect or sterilize reusable equipment/ devices according to the manufacturer’s instructions, national or international standards, /using efficient methods and based on intended use.
Safe or unsafe practice?

items.text: Discarding the sharps container when three-quarters full
Wearing the same gloves between two babies
Leaving a needle in the septum of a vial
Cleaning frequently touched surfaces at least daily

read.explanation: From the manual's lists for gloves, safe injections and environmental cleaning.

sections.title: Preventing sepsis: manual disinfection of equipment

read.text: Manual Disinfection Prepare the decontamination station

• (bench of 2 meters) and using 4 containers (size 10 litters) labelled as following:
      • The first container contains water and soap
      • Second container contains water
      • Third container contains working solution of chlorine-based solution in concentration (0.1% w/v).
      • Forth container contains sterile or filter water.
Manual disinfection steps:

• 1. Wear a clean glove, collect used dirty items to be disinfect, wrap it in a towel or container, transfer it to decontamination room or designated area.
  • 2. Unwrap the items in dirty surface, wipe the items using a clean towel to remove secretions, it prefers to disinfect each tool or devices in a separate.
  • 3. Unassembled all parts of items (e.g., ambubag).
  • 4. Remove the gloves, wash hands, wear appropriate PPE (apron, google, medical mask, heavy duty gloves).
  • 5. Wash all part of items to remove a dirt, using different size and shapes of brushes, brushing under water level to prevent splash of aerosol.
  • 6. Then rinse items in water of container 2 to remove soap residue.
  • 7. Remove heavy duty gloves and wash hands, wear a clean gloves take off items from water, dry it using a clean towel or gauze.
  • 8. Transfer all objects to chlorine container, and covers it, ensure it all under solution level.
  • 9. Wait for 20 mins, using sterile forceps transfer objects into container 4, to remove excess chlorine.
  • 10. Prepare sterile surface or tray, wear sterile gloves, remove items from water in container 4 and dry it by sterile gauze or towel.
  • 11. Reassemble all items and check for functionality.
  • 12. Store the disinfected items in sterile container or box, or wrap in sterile towel, label it as (disinfected / date).
  • 13. Change the chlorine solution daily.
In the decontamination station, how strong is the chlorine and how long do items stay in it?
read.explanation: Four containers: soap and water, water, 0.1% chlorine, sterile or filtered water. Change the chlorine solution daily.
