exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 1 — The Cold Baby from the Rural Health Centre
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 3 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 2917)
narrative: A 2-hour-old male newborn is brought to the neonatal unit by a midwife from a rural health centre. He was born at 38 weeks by spontaneous vaginal delivery, but the delivery room was cold and immediate drying and warming were inadequate. The baby did not cry at birth and required brief stimulation, after which he had irregular breathing.
On arrival he appears lethargic and unresponsive to handling. His skin feels cold, and there is blue discolouration of the lips and tongue.

Vital signs: HR 160 bpm, RR 77/min, SpO₂ 72%, axillary temperature 35.2°C. The extremities are cold, capillary refill time is 4 seconds, and the pulse is weak and rapid. He has apnoeic episodes with occasional gasping respirations, severe chest retractions and an audible expiratory grunt.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Classification: EMERGENCY. He has almost every emergency sign at once — hypothermia below 36°C, apnoea and gasping, severe respiratory distress (rate above 70 with severe retractions and grunt), central cyanosis, and shock (cold periphery, CRT 4 seconds, weak fast pulse).
First actions: manage the airway, tactile stimulation, PPV for the gasping, give oxygen, start re- warming, insert an IV line and give 10 ml/kg normal saline over 30 minutes, check the glucose.
Stabilize, then admit to the SCNU.
Teaching point: this baby is cold because of what happened in the delivery room two hours ago.
Everything else on this list follows from that. The golden minute and the golden hour are not separate from triage — they are why this baby is in front of you.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 2 — The Baby with the Omphalocele
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 3 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 2941)
narrative: A 6-hour-old male newborn is brought to the unit after delivery at a rural health facility. He was born by spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 20-year-old primigravida with no antenatal care. The mother reports the baby cried weakly at birth and has been “not looking well” since.
On arrival he appears small and fragile, birth weight 1.6 kg. He has a large omphalocele with bowel loops visible, covered by a thin sac.

Findings: the baby is cold and irritable. PR 120 bpm, SpO₂ 90% on room air, temperature 36.2°C, RR 68/min, no chest retractions or grunting. The abdomen is distended and the omphalocele is prominent. The skin and sclera are deeply jaundiced. There is severe pallor with pale mucous membranes and delayed capillary refill, oozing of blood from the umbilical stump, and mild bleeding from a heel-prick site.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Classification: PRIORITY — and read the list carefully, because this baby collects almost every priority sign there is: cold stress (36.2°C, between 36 and 36.5), respiratory distress with rate above 60 and no retractions, irritable, abdominal distension, severe jaundice, severe pallor, bleeding from more than one site, a major congenital malformation, and weight under 1.8 kg.

But: check the capillary refill and the pulse volume carefully. ‘Delayed capillary refill’ with severe pallor and active bleeding is the edge of shock. If CRT is over 3 seconds with a weak fast pulse, this becomes an EMERGENCY.

Actions: assess and act rapidly, admit to the SCNU. Cover the omphalocele with warm sterile saline gauze and plastic wrap — do not let it dry, and remember it is a huge route of heat and fluid loss. NG tube for the distended abdomen. Vitamin K and investigate the bleeding. Check the glucose and the haemoglobin. Warm the baby.
Teaching point: a baby can be ‘priority’ on paper and slipping into ‘emergency’ while you write.
Triage is not done once. Re-triage the baby who is waiting.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 3 — The One-Day-Old from the Maternity Ward
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 3 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 2968)
narrative: A 1-day-old newborn arrives from the maternity ward. The baby is cold, not feeding, and breathing fast.

questions.question: Q1. Is this an emergency? Q2. What action must be taken immediately? Q3. Where should this baby be managed?
points: Emergency. Immediate stabilization. SCBU / NICU admission.

Note how little information you were given — and note that you did not need any more. Cold, not feeding, breathing fast is enough to act on. Waiting for the full history is one of the three common errors.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 4 — The Baby Who Can Wait
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 3 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 2982)
narrative: A 3-day-old term baby, birth weight 3.1 kg, brought by the mother because he is “yellow”. He is feeding well and is active. Temperature 36.8°C, RR 48/min, no indrawing, no grunting. There is mild jaundice of the face and chest, and a small cephalhaematoma. The cord is clean and dry.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Classification: NON-URGENT. Jaundice and minor birth trauma are both on the non-urgent list. He is feeding, warm, and not distressed.

Action: assess fully and counsel the parents. That does not mean send them away — it means take a proper history, examine the baby, measure the bilirubin according to your protocol, and teach the mother the danger signs and when to come back immediately.
Teaching point: ‘non-urgent’ does not mean ‘not important’. It means this baby does not need your hands in the next 60 seconds. It still needs your attention today.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Exercise : Writing admission order
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 3 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026
narrative: Give each small group the clinical details of Case 1 or Case 2 from Session 2.
Each group writes a full admission order set on a blank order sheet, using the nine headings above.
Groups then swap sheets. The receiving group plays the two reviewing nurses.
The reviewing group must find and challenge: anything unclear, any missing system, any dose they cannot verify.

questions.question: Q1. What are the key steps you would follow, in order? Q2. What are the common mistakes to avoid, and how would you prevent them?
points: System Expected order Level of care Intensive care CNS Monitor for encephalopathy and seizures; consider cranial imaging when stable CVS Continuous monitoring. Normal saline 10 ml/kg over 30 min, reassess.

Consider inotropes if shock persists after boluses Respiratory PPV → CPAP or ventilation per response. State FiO₂ and settings. Blood gas now and in 4 hours. Chest X-ray GIT NPO. NG tube on free drainage Renal and fluid TFI 60 ml/kg/day day 1, 10% dextrose. Monitor urine output hourly Infectious diseases Blood culture before antibiotics. Ampicillin + gentamicin Procedures UVC for access. LP deferred until stable Medications Vitamin K. Dextrose bolus if glucose low, then infusion Accept any clinically sound variation — what is being assessed is whether every heading was addressed and whether the orders are unambiguous.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 1 — Where Does He Belong?
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 3397)
narrative: A baby is born at 35 weeks, birth weight 1.9 kg. He is pink, active, temperature 36.8°C, RR 48/min with no indrawing. He attaches at the breast and sucks for a few minutes, then tires.

questions.question: Q1. Is he preterm, LBW, or both? Classify him by both systems. Q2. Where should he be cared for? Q3. What exactly do you do?
points: Classification: moderate to late preterm (32 to < 36 6/7 weeks) AND low birth weight (1500– 2500 g). Both.
Place of care: birth weight > 1.8 kg → postnatal ward WITH the mother. He does not need a nursery bed.

What you do: monitor — and train the mother. KMC and temperature assessment by touch; breastfeeding and milk expression; LBW feeding content and technique; recognition and reporting of danger signs. Vitamin K 1 mg IM (he is ≥ 1000 g). Delay bathing.
The catch: ‘he tires’. Watch him. If he becomes unable to feed from breast or cup, or becomes sick, he is admitted to the nursery immediately — regardless of the 1.9 kg.
questions.explain: the weight decides the starting place. The baby decides whether he stays there.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 3 — Same Weight, Different Baby
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 3444)
narrative: Two babies arrive in your unit in the same hour. Both weigh 1.7 kg.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Baby A: preterm, appropriate for gestational age. LBW because he is early.

Baby B: term SGA with asymmetrical IUGR — long, thin, alert, marasmic, excess skin folds, ponderal index < 2, head circumference exceeding chest by more than 3 cm, meconium staining, placental insufficiency from the pre-eclampsia. LBW because he did not grow.
RDS: Baby A — immature lungs. Baby B has term lungs.
Hypoglycaemia: BOTH — but for different reasons. A has not laid down glycogen yet; B has used his up. B may be the more brittle.
Hypothermia: BOTH — A has no fat and thin skin; B has no fat either. Little surface insulation on a large surface area.
Place: both are 1.5–1.8 kg → Level II. Same place, same weight — completely different watch lists.
questions.explain: never let the scale do your thinking. Two babies at 1.7 kg are not the same problem.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 4 — Day 5, Something Has Changed
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 3481)
narrative: A 28-week baby, now 5 days old, 1.1 kg, has been stable on CPAP in your unit. This morning the nurse reports three apnoeic episodes in the last hour, each needing stimulation. He had been having none. He is on caffeine. Temperature 36.9°C. Feeds have been going in but there were 2 ml of green aspirate this morning and the abdomen looks fuller.

questions.question: Q1. Is this ‘just apnoea of prematurity’? Q2. What is your list? What do you check? Q3. What is the green aspirate telling you?
points: No. He was not having apnoeas; now he is. A CHANGE in a stable preterm is never ‘just prematurity’. Apnoea of prematurity does not start on day 5 in a baby already on caffeine.
The list to exclude: sepsis, hypoxaemia, shock · IVH, seizures · PDA · anaemia · drugs · hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia · temperature · obstruction · reflux.

The green aspirate plus a fuller abdomen plus new apnoea: think NEC and think sepsis. Stop feeds, NG tube on free drainage, blood culture, antibiotics, abdominal X-ray, check glucose, check haemoglobin. Look for a PDA murmur.
The trap in this case: increasing the caffeine dose and going back to the ward round. Every group has someone who does this. Let the debrief say it, not you.
questions.explain: new apnoea in a preterm is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Find out what it is a symptom OF.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 1 — “He Is Too Small For That”
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 3986)
narrative: A baby is born at 30 weeks, 1.1 kg. He is breathing with grunting, on CPAP, and has an IV line.
At 40 minutes of age the mother asks whether she can hold him. The doctor says: “not yet — he is only 1.1 kg and he is not stable. Maybe in a week, when he is bigger.

questions.question: Q1. Is the doctor right? Quote the protocol. Q2. What are the ONLY two reasons to delay skin-to-skin at birth? Q3. What has this baby lost in the last 40 minutes?
points: The doctor is wrong on both counts. Weight is NOT a barrier to initiation. KMC is safe for both stable and unstable babies. ‘When he is bigger’ is exactly backwards — the smallest, sickest babies gain the most.

The only two exceptions: the baby is haemodynamically unstable or unable to breathe; or the mother is critically ill and no substitute caregiver is available. He is breathing, on CPAP, with a line. He does not meet either exception.
What he has lost: immediate KMC significantly reduces mortality, particularly within the first 72 hours. He is in the window right now, and he is spending it alone.
What should happen: skin-to-skin now, with the CPAP and the line arranged without tangles.
Attempt the breast; if not, colostrum within the first hour.
questions.explain: ‘too small’ and ‘too sick’ are the two commonest reasons given for withholding KMC — and they are the two strongest reasons for providing it.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 1 — The Feed That Was Never Started
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 4523)
narrative: A 1.1 kg baby, 29 weeks, now 4 days old. He is stable on CPAP. He has had IV fluids only since birth. The notes say each day: “Nil by mouth — on CPAP.” His mother has not been shown how to express and says her breasts are now soft and comfortable.

questions.question: Q1. What has gone wrong, and on which day? Q2. Does CPAP prevent feeding? Q3. What has happened to the milk supply, and what do you do about it?
points: What went wrong: trophic feeding should have started within the FIRST 24 HOURS in a stable baby, and progression no later than DAY 4. He has had neither. Four days of gut rest in a 29- weeker is four days of villous atrophy and lost time.

CPAP does not prevent feeding. It changes the TUBE — orogastric is preferred in preterms on nasal CPAP, because nasogastric tubes interfere with ease of breathing. ‘Nil by mouth — on CPAP’ is not a clinical decision, it is a habit.

The milk supply: ‘soft and comfortable’ on day 4 means the supply is failing. Breast milk production relies on supply and demand; without frequent expression and complete emptying, it stops. This is urgent — start intensive expression support today, every 2–3 hours including overnight, with skin-to-skin.
What you do now: start trophic feeds via OG tube today; begin expression support immediately; put him in KMC; document a daily feeding plan so it cannot drift again.
The trap: groups focus on the baby and miss the mother. The milk supply is the harder problem and the one with the shorter window.
questions.explain: ‘Nil by mouth’ written four days running is not a plan. Every day without a feeding decision is a decision.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 2 — The Feed That Was Pushed
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 4551)
narrative: A nurse is feeding a 1.4 kg baby by OG tube. The ward is busy. She attaches the syringe with the plunger in, pushes the 18 mL feed in over about 30 seconds, and moves on. Ten minutes later the baby is found desaturated with milk at the mouth.

questions.question: Q1. What happened? Q2. What are the immediate actions? Q3. What do you say to the nurse — and what do you say to the unit?
points: What happened: the feed was PUSHED. The manual is explicit — it is dangerous to push milk using the plunger; it may lead to respiratory aspiration and severe complications. A rapid bolus into a small stomach caused reflux and probable aspiration.
Immediate actions: position, suction the mouth, assess airway and breathing, oxygen and support as needed, call for help. Stop feeds and assess. Consider chest X-ray. Watch for aspiration pneumonia.

To the nurse: not blame — the manual says this happens under time pressure. Show her the technique WITH the plunger out, hands together, and let her do it. She is more likely to change with a demonstration than a reprimand.

To the unit: this is a system finding, not an individual one (cross-reference Patient Safety, Swiss-cheese model). Why was the ward so busy? Are the syringes the right type? Is the gravity rule in the written feeding policy? Is it taught at orientation?
The single most preventable feeding injury in any newborn unit. It takes 30 seconds to cause and it is entirely avoided by removing a piece of plastic.
questions.explain: gravity, not pressure. The plunger stays out.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 3 — The Residual
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 4578)
narrative: A 1.2 kg baby, day 9, on 100 mL/kg/day by OG tube and tolerating well. At the 6 a.m. feed the nurse aspirates routinely and finds 4 mL of milky residual from a 15 mL feed. The abdomen is soft, the baby is pink, active and afebrile. She withholds the feed and documents “feed intolerance”.

questions.question: Q1. Was the aspiration indicated? Q2. Is 4 mL from a 15 mL feed significant? Q3. Was withholding correct?
points: The aspiration was NOT indicated. Routine gastric residual checks do more harm than good — they disrupt acid production, increase infection risk, deactivate pepsin, and worsen intolerance.
Check GRV ONLY if there are clear signs of GI pathology. This baby had none.
The volume: 4 mL of 15 mL is about 27% — below the 30% threshold, not bile or blood stained, with a benign abdominal exam. By the grading table this is LOW: continue feeding, monitor and follow up.

Withholding was WRONG on both counts: the test should not have been done, and the result did not meet the threshold for action. Do not stop feeding a baby because of a GRV unless the baby also shows clear signs of illness — bile-stained vomit, severe distension, bloody stools, or systemic instability.
The system question: why did she aspirate? Almost certainly because the feeding chart has an ‘aspirate’ column. The chart is teaching the old practice every shift. Change the chart.
Every group will debate the 4 mL. The more important answer is that the number should never have been generated. The finding drives the test, not the timetable.
questions.explain: a missed feed is a real harm. Do not create a reason to miss one.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 4 — No Fortifier
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 4606)
narrative: A 1.3 kg baby, 31 weeks, day 14, on full expressed breast milk at 150 mL/kg/day and tolerating well. Weight gain is 8 g/day. Serum urea is 1.4 mmol/L. The unit has no commercial human milk fortifier and none is expected.

questions.question: Q1. What is the urea telling you? Q2. Is his weight gain adequate? Q3. What are your options, in order?
points: The urea: 1.4 mmol/L is below 1.8 — which indicates TOO LITTLE PROTEIN in the diet. The action stated in the manual is to consider increasing milk volume or fortifying feeds.
Weight gain: 8 g/day is below the preterm target of 15–20 g/day. The biochemistry and the growth chart agree — he is underfed.

Options in order: (1) fortify EBM using newborn standard formula or premature formula; (2) if nothing is available, increase EBM volume to 200 mL/kg/day divided into 8 feeds, under close medical supervision to avoid fluid overload; (3) 220 mL/kg/day may be considered ONLY IF PDA, congenital cardiac conditions and chronic lung disease are excluded.

Before increasing volume: examine for a murmur and signs of PDA, review the respiratory history for chronic lung disease, and document the exclusion. And note the ceiling — do not exceed 200 mL/kg/day without senior specialist consultation.
questions.explain: no fortifier is not no options. But the volume route has an explicit safety gate, and that gate is three diagnoses you must actively exclude and write down.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 5 — The Baby Who Said No
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 4631)
narrative: A 1.9 kg baby, 34 weeks, has been on tube feeds and is now being offered the breast. He roots and latches. After two minutes he goes quiet, then pale; his nostrils flare and he coughs. The mother is anxious and asks whether she should keep trying — “he was doing so well.

questions.question: Q1. What are you seeing? Q2. Do you continue? Q3. What do you say to the mother?
points: What you are seeing: suck–swallow–breathe incoordination with STOP signs — colour change (pale), increased work of breathing (nasal flaring), and clinical distress (coughing). He rooted and latched, which are readiness CUES, but cues alone are not enough; the physiological stability is what failed.
Do you continue? NO. If the baby shows stress signals during an attempt, STOP THE ORAL FEED ATTEMPT ENTIRELY. Continuing risks choking and aspiration.

What you say to the mother: not ‘he failed’. He showed you exactly what he could manage today and told you when to stop — which is a good sign, not a bad one. Complete this feed by tube in the KMC position, keep offering non-nutritive suckling at the emptied breast, and try again at the next feed. Reassure her the supply is protected by continuing to express.
The trap: ‘he was doing so well’ is the sentence that makes people push on. Rooting and latching are the easy part; the coordination is what matures last.
questions.explain: stopping is not failure. The baby is allowed to say no, and hearing it the first time is the skill.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 1 — Baby 1
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026
narrative: Term, 38 weeks, 40 hours old. TSB 240 µmol/L. No risk factors.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Answer: Plot 240 µmol/L at 40 hours on the phototherapy threshold chart for ≥ 38 weeks with no risk factors. This sits BELOW the phototherapy line. Action: no phototherapy; repeat TSB and reassess. The teaching point — a number that sounds high is not high for this age.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 2 — Baby 2
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026
narrative: Term, 38 weeks, 18 hours old. TSB 180 µmol/L.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Answer: The plot matters less than the CLOCK. This baby is jaundiced at 18 hours — under 24 hours — which is pathological by definition, whatever the chart says. Action: start phototherapy per the chart AND investigate the cause (Coombs, blood groups, FBC, retics, G6PD). Every

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 3 — Baby 3
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026
narrative: 35 weeks, 30 hours old, TSB 220 µmol/L, Coombs positive, mother O negative.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Answer: 35 weeks WITH risk factors — use the lower (risk-factor) threshold line, not the term line. Coombs positive means isoimmune haemolysis. Action: start phototherapy at the lower threshold; recheck TSB in 6 hours; watch the RATE of rise; consider IVIG (500–1000 mg/kg over 2 hours) if TSB keeps rising despite phototherapy; prepare for possible exchange.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 4 — Baby 4
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026
narrative: Term, 60 hours old. TSB was 280 µmol/L at 54 hours, now 340 µmol/L. Already on phototherapy.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Answer: Calculate the RATE: 60 µmol/L in 6 hours = 10 µmol/L/hr. That exceeds 8.5 µmol/L/hr (0.5 mg/dL/hr) DESPITE intensive phototherapy — an exchange transfusion indication. Action: escalate to tertiary now; cross-match blood; do not wait for the next level to be crossed.
Baby 4 is the case that teaches the rate. Two numbers and a clock give you a slope, and the slope

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 1 — The Day-One Baby Who Looks Well
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 4996)
narrative: A term baby, 3.2 kg, normal delivery, is noticed to be slightly yellow at 20 hours of age. He is feeding, active, afebrile. The midwife says: “He is only a bit yellow and he is feeding beautifully — all babies go yellow, we will look again tomorrow.

questions.question: Q1. Is the midwife right? Q2. What does the timing tell you? Q3. What happens next — exactly?
points: The midwife is wrong. Jaundice within the first 24 hours is NEVER physiological. ‘He looks well’ is not reassurance — he looks well now, and bilirubin rises.

What happens next: measure TSB now and plot against age in hours. Investigate the cause — blood group (mother and baby), Coombs, FBC and reticulocytes, G6PD. Start phototherapy per the nomogram. Do not wait for tomorrow.
The thinking error: using the baby's appearance instead of the clock. The 24-hour rule is a rule precisely because well-looking babies with early jaundice are the ones who get missed.
questions.explain: in the first 24 hours, the clock overrules the eye.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 2 — The Referral That Did Not Happen
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 5016)
narrative: A 36-week baby, 2.2 kg, born at a health centre. Day 3. Deep jaundice including the palms and soles. Feeding poorly, sleepy. The health centre has no bilirubinometer. The nearest district hospital is two hours away and the family has no transport money.

questions.question: Q1. Which referral criteria are met? Q2. What can the health centre do while arranging transfer? Q3. What must be communicated to the district hospital?
points: Referral criteria met — FOUR: deep jaundice especially palms and soles; poor feeding and lethargy; preterm; low birth weight. Any ONE of these was enough.
While arranging transfer: keep the baby warm; support feeding/hydration; document the age in HOURS and the time jaundice was first seen; do not delay transfer to ‘observe’.
Communicate: age in hours, when jaundice was first noticed, feeding history, risk factors (preterm, LBW), and that no TSB is available. Use SBAR (cross-reference Patient Safety).

The real issue: ‘no transport money’ is a clinical problem here, not a social one. This is the Sudan-specific delay the manual names. Ask the group how their own units solve it — and whether anyone has a written referral-support pathway.
questions.explain: at primary level you cannot measure bilirubin — but you can measure the clock, the feeding and the palms. All three said refer, on day one of noticing.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 3 — The Rate, Not the Number
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 5039)
narrative: A 38-week baby on intensive phototherapy since 48 hours. At 54 hours TSB was 280 µmol/L. At 60 hours it is 340 µmol/L. The registrar says: “Still under the exchange line — keep the lights on and recheck in the morning.

questions.question: Q1. Calculate the rate of rise. Q2. Is the registrar right? Q3. What do you do now?
points: The rate: 340 − 280 = 60 µmol/L over 6 hours = 10 µmol/L per hour.

The registrar is wrong. A rise of ≥ 8.5 µmol/L/hr (≥ 0.5 mg/dL/hr) DESPITE intensive phototherapy is itself an exchange transfusion indication. Ten exceeds 8.5. He does not need to cross the line — the slope has already answered.

What you do now: escalate to tertiary; cross-match fresh, irradiated, leukocyte-depleted blood; continue intensive phototherapy meanwhile; check for haemolysis (Coombs, G6PD) and consider IVIG if isoimmune; correct glucose, calcium and acidosis in preparation.
The trap: ‘still under the line’ is the most dangerous sentence in jaundice management. The threshold is where you must act; the slope is where you should act.
questions.explain: two numbers and a clock give you a slope. The slope decides before the threshold does.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 4 — The Baby Who Is Telling You
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 5 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 5061)
narrative: A 4-day-old term baby, deeply jaundiced, brought from home. He is lethargic, will not feed, has a high-pitched cry, and arches backwards when handled. The laboratory is closed and no TSB is available until morning.

questions.question: Q1. What are you looking at? Q2. Does the absence of a bilirubin level change anything? Q3. What is the immediate management?
points: This is ACUTE BILIRUBIN ENCEPHALOPATHY. Lethargy, poor feeding, high-pitched cry and opisthotonus are the named signs. This is bilirubin in the brain, now.

The missing TSB changes NOTHING. Exchange transfusion is urgent REGARDLESS OF BILIRUBIN LEVEL when there are signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. Waiting for a number until morning is waiting while the injury completes.

Immediate management: intensive phototherapy immediately, while everything else is arranged. Call the consultant. Arrange urgent cross-matched blood. Establish access (UVC preferred). Correct hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia and acidosis. Prepare for exchange. Treat any underlying cause — sepsis screen, Coombs, G6PD.
Also: this baby needs long-term follow-up — hearing test and neurodevelopmental assessment — whatever happens tonight.
Every group will ask about the bilirubin level. That question is the teaching moment: the baby IS the result. Signs of encephalopathy authorise action on their own.
questions.explain: when the brain is already showing you the diagnosis, the laboratory is not the decision-maker.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 3 — The Wrap Is Wrong
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 6 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 4036)
narrative: You walk into the KMC room. A mother is sitting with her 1.5 kg baby skin-to-skin. She has tied the wrap firmly and neatly — it is snug across the baby's back and abdomen. The baby's chin is resting down on his own chest. He is quiet. She is proud of how well she has secured him and says he has not moved in an hour.

questions.question: Q1. What do you see? Q2. Which two positioning steps have been broken? Q3. What do you say to her?
points: Two errors, both dangerous: (1) The chin is down on the chest — the neck is FLEXED. Step 5: the head must be secured at ear level, preventing hyperextension or flexion, to avoid obstructive apnoea. (2) The wrap is snug across the abdomen — Step 6: the diaphragm must be able to move freely to enable unrestricted breathing.
‘He has not moved in an hour’ is not reassurance. In this position, it is the finding.

What you say: not ‘you did it wrong’. She has done something hard and she has done most of it well. Reposition WITH her — head to the side in the sniffing position, ear level, loosen over the belly, watch the abdomen move together. Then have her show you. Praise the securing; fix the airway.
The trap in this case: a participant who says ‘tell her to redo it’ and walks on. Coaching is done with your hands next to hers, not from the doorway.
questions.explain: a neat wrap and a safe wrap are not the same thing. Ear level, and let the belly move.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 4 — The Alarm at 2 a.m.
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 6 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 4061)
narrative: A mother in the KMC step-down ward wakes at 2 a.m. Her 1.6 kg baby, 34 weeks, feels limp and she thinks he stopped breathing for a few seconds. She has been taught the danger signs. She is frightened.

questions.question: Q1. What should she do — exactly? Q2. Which danger signs are present? Q3. What is the one thing she should NOT do?
points: Danger signs present: apnoea (any episode requiring stimulation, or > 20 seconds) and lethargy/floppiness (baby feels limp). Two of the six.
What she does: call immediately for medical assistance WHILE KEEPING THE BABY IN THE SKIN-TO-SKIN POSITION.
What she must NOT do: take him off her chest and carry him to find a nurse. That makes him colder and less stable. The position stays unless he needs emergency resuscitation.

And note: she has been coached in CPR for apnoea or sudden collapse. That is in the skill coaching row. If he needs stimulation, she can give it in the first seconds — which is where the seconds matter.
Then the team: this is new apnoea in a preterm — it is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Exclude sepsis, hypoglycaemia, temperature, anaemia, IVH, PDA.
questions.explain: teaching the mother the danger signs is not a formality on a discharge form. She is the monitor for 18 hours a day. Teach her properly and she will find things before your machine does.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Case 5 — Ready to Go?
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 6 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 4086)
narrative: A 1.9 kg baby, born at 34 weeks, now 10 days old. He has regained his birthweight and gained 20 g/day for the last 4 days. He is off the gastric tube and finishing his cup feeds. Vital signs normal, no danger signs. He breastfeeds for a while then tires, and finishes by cup.
His mother is 17 years old. She practises KMC when reminded. She can breastfeed but has not cup-fed him herself — the nurses do it. She has not been taught CPR. Her own mother lives three hours away.

questions.question: Q1. Does the BABY meet the discharge criteria? Q2. Does the PAIR meet the discharge criteria? Q3. What must happen before he goes?
points: The baby: yes. ≤ 1.8 kg row — regained birthweight, > 34 weeks, consistent weight gain ≥ 3 days averaging 20 g/day, off the gastric tube and doing well on cup feeds. Able to breastfeed directly and finish expressed milk by cup. Normal vitals, no danger signs. He is ready.

The pair: NO. Read the mother row. She must practise KMC CONSISTENTLY — she does it when reminded. She must be skilled in direct breast- AND cup-feeding — she has never cup-fed him. She must be educated on danger signs and CPR — she has not been. She is not a discharge criterion that has been met.

What must happen: she cup-feeds him herself, repeatedly, until she is skilled. She is taught the danger signs and CPR. She is taught the four checks. And — because she is very young — identify a supporting family member. Her mother is three hours away; who else?

Before he goes she gets, in writing: the multivitamin and iron prescription, the discharge date and weight on the documents or immunization card, the feeding instructions for home, and the date and place of the first follow-up visit. He is immunized with a document and a next date.
Follow-up at 1 week, 2 weeks, 1 month, then monthly to 3 kg or 40 weeks corrected.

The trap: every group discharges this baby. He looks perfect on the weight chart. Discharging him is discharging a 17-year-old who has never fed her own baby, three hours from her mother, into a home where he must stay in KMC until 2.5–3 kg.
questions.explain: discharge criteria focus on feeding competence and maternal readiness — NOT on weight alone.

exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 9 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 7161)
narrative: A 1.5 kg preterm baby received 10 TIMES the intended antibiotic dose, due to a decimal error.

questions.question: Q1. Ask: where did the system fail? What could have prevented it?
points: Answer key — the layers that should have caught it: the prescriber's calculation (three- quarters of neonatal medication errors occur at the PRESCRIBING stage); the pre-administration routine; the independent double-check by a second person; a unit formulary or emergency dose sheet listing the correct dose by weight; adequate lighting and freedom from interruption at the point of preparation. A tenfold decimal error passes only when ALL of these are missing or skipped at once.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M2 · Scenario: over three weeks, eight babies in your
exercises.source: Manual Module (2) Special Newborn Care, Section 10 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026
narrative: unit were treated for sepsis and two died.
Roles:

NICU nurse in-charge Medical officer Laboratory focal person Infection control focal person The team demonstrates the surveillance workflow: what data are collected · how cases are detected and reported · how laboratory samples (blood, CSF, swab) contribute to confirmation · how findings guide IPC actions and quality improvement.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Objective What the team should have shown 1 — Incidence They counted. Eight cases and two deaths in three weeks is a NUMBER, and it is compared against something 2 — Risk factors They looked for what the eight shared — gestation, weight, lines, ventilation, day of onset, which nurse, which incubator 3 — Sensitivity Cultures were taken BEFORE antibiotics; isolates and sensitivities were collated, not just filed 4 — IPC effectiveness They asked what changed before the run started, and what they will change now — and how they will know if it worked 5 — Benchmarking Data go somewhere. To the hospital, to the state, and back to the unit 6 — Outbreak response Same organism in a cluster = outbreak until proved otherwise. Report to the hospital infection control committee to search for cases in other departments
